title: Non-object tool-call arguments crash the entire agent run instead of self-correcting
description: Agent#parse_arguments (agent.rb:1364-1373) returns whatever JSON.parse produces. It only special-cases unparseable JSON (:invalid_json). If the model emits tool arguments that are VALID JSON but not an object ("[]", "5", "\"ship it\""), the non-Hash value flows into ToolExecutor#execute, whose first line is `(input || {}).transform_keys(&:to_s)` (tool_executor.rb:199). Array/String/Integer have no transform_keys, so NoMethodError is raised OUTSIDE invoke_tool_handler's rescue, propagates through run_tool_calls and run_loop, and escapes Agent#respond, which rescues only OllamaClient::Error (agent.rb:288). For read_code_file it can also raise earlier in guarded_code_read_result via `args["path"]` on an Integer.
failure_or_value: GLM tool-calling occasionally emits non-object arguments (e.g. an empty array for a no-arg tool). One such call kills the whole run mid-flight: the in-app copilot request 500s (ask_savant_controller.rb has no rescue), a Slack turn falls to the generic outer rescue and Brian gets a raw failure message, and all the run's prior tool work is thrown away. A malformed-STRING argument, by contrast, gets the friendly 'resend valid JSON' error and the model self-corrects; this identical failure mode just crashes.
fix_sketch: In Agent#parse_arguments, after JSON.parse succeeds, return :invalid_json unless the parsed value is a Hash: `parsed = JSON.parse(stripped); parsed.is_a?(Hash) ? parsed : :invalid_json`. That routes the case into the existing 'Your tool arguments were not valid JSON. Resend the call with a single valid JSON object.' feedback path so the model retries correctly. Optionally also harden ToolExecutor#execute with `input = input.is_a?(Hash) ? input.transform_keys(&:to_s) : {}` as belt-and-braces.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every link in the chain. Agent#parse_arguments (agent.rb:1364-1373) rescues only JSON::ParserError, so valid non-object JSON ("[]", "5", "\"ship it\"", "true") returns an Array/Integer/String/Boolean. run_tool_calls (agent.rb:426-431) special-cases only :invalid_json; tellingly, its observer calls already guard with `args.is_a?(Hash) ? args : {}` (lines 415/422) while the execution path at 431 passes raw args through. ToolExecutor#execute's first line `(input || {}).transform_keys(&:to_s)` (tool_executor.rb:199) raises NoMethodError for any non-Hash BEFORE invoke_tool_handler's rescue is reached; read_code_file dies even earlier via `args["path"]` on an Array (agent.rb:600, TypeError). No rescue exists in run_tool_calls or run_loop, and Agent#respond rescues only OllamaClient::Error (agent.rb:288). OllamaClient.chat returns raw provider JSON with no tool_calls sanitization. Blast radius verified: AskSavantController#create (line 22) has no rescue so the copilot request 500s; Slack::EventProcessor's generic rescue (line 75) posts the raw 'internal error' fallback and discards the run's tool work; ScheduledAgentRunJob fails the run. Concrete input: a model turn with function.arguments = "[]" deterministically crashes the run. Downgraded from high to medium only because the trigger is intermittent model misbehavior, not attacker-controlled or data-corrupting, and runs recover on retry; the code path itself is deterministic once the input occurs.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. The fix (`parsed.is_a?(Hash) ? parsed : :invalid_json` in parse_arguments) routes the case into the existing 'resend valid JSON' feedback loop that already exists for malformed strings, so the model self-corrects instead of the run dying — strictly better behavior, no new code paths. touches_client_email=false: nothing near SponsorPortalMailer/SponsorAssetReminderService or any sponsor-facing send. No /api/v1 fields renamed/removed, no schema changes, no behavior change for well-formed tool calls. The belt-and-braces executor coercion (non-Hash → {}) is also safe but slightly worse alone since it silently drops the model's malformed intent instead of prompting a retry; prefer the parse_arguments fix as primary. Add unit specs for parse_arguments non-object inputs and run the full rspec suite; the existing green suite has no coverage of this path so no pre-existing tests should be affected.

title: ConfirmationGate authorizes external sends off incidental words: mid-message affirmatives and noun-form 'reply' bypass the preview
description: Two gaps in the gate that fronts send_mail/reply_mail/merge on the Slack surface. (1) affirmative? (line 130) matches AFFIRMATIVES ('yes', 'yeah', 'ok', 'sure', line 38-42) ANYWHERE in the inbound message, so a conversational 'yeah' or 'ok' embedded in a long instruction authorizes whatever consequential action the model attempts that turn. (2) send_directive? (line 124-128) treats any SEND_VERBS hit ('reply', 'respond', 'follow up with') as authorization, and the COMPOSE_CONTEXT guard ('draft', 'prepare', 'write up') only tempers EMAIL_WORDS, not SEND_VERBS, so noun/compose usages of 'reply' still authorize a real send.
failure_or_value: Brian in Slack: 'yeah I saw that. draft a reply to the Acme folks for me to review first.' — 'yeah' matches AFFIRMATIVES and 'reply' matches SEND_VERBS, so ConfirmationGate returns :authorized and reply_mail sends the draft to the external recipient immediately, with no preview, despite 'for me to review first'. The system prompt is the only remaining defense; the coded gate (the defense-in-depth layer Brian relies on) is open.
fix_sketch: In confirmation_gate.rb: (a) apply the COMPOSE_CONTEXT suppression to SEND_VERBS the same way it applies to EMAIL_WORDS in send_directive? (a message containing draft/compose/prepare/write-up context should not read 'reply' as a send directive); (b) in affirmative?, only accept a bare affirmative when the message is short (e.g. text.length <= 40) or begins with the affirmative phrase, so a mid-paragraph 'ok'/'yeah' never authorizes. Keep directives ('send it', 'ship it') matching anywhere as today. Add gate specs for the 'draft a reply ... to review' and 'yeah I saw that ...' shapes.

verdict.reason: Reproduced on the actual code: in confirmation_gate.rb, send_directive? (line 124-128) applies the COMPOSE_CONTEXT suppression only to EMAIL_WORDS, so "draft a reply to acme" returns :authorized while the spec (confirmation_gate_spec.rb:26-30) asserts the equivalent "draft an email to acme" must be :needs_confirmation — the code contradicts its own tested intent. And affirmative? (line 130) matches AFFIRMATIVES anywhere, so "yeah i saw that. draft a reply to the acme folks for me to review first." authorizes via both "yeah" and "reply" (verified by running the gate's exact regex/negation-window logic on that input; no STOP_SIGNAL or negation applies). The result is live-wired: tool_executor.rb confirmation_block (line 4764) returns nil on :authorized and send_mail (line 1868) / reply_mail (line 1960) proceed to a real external send; the remaining pre-send checks validate content, not intent. Caveat keeping this from critical: the misfire requires the model to wrongly attempt the send tool that turn — but defending against exactly that is the gate's stated purpose, and "draft a reply" is a routine Brian phrasing, so the coded safety layer is open on a common path.
verdict.ship_risk: Low-to-medium, and fail-safe in direction. The fix is contained to ConfirmationGate: tightening it can only convert a would-be send into a preview-and-confirm round-trip, never the reverse. Main regression risk is over-suppression: a legit mixed message like "prepare the deck and send it to acme" contains both COMPOSE_CONTEXT ("prepare") and a send verb, so a blanket suppression would gate a real directive — annoying (extra confirmation) but safe; consider suppressing only when the send verb appears in noun form or in the same clause as the compose word, and keep explicit directives ("send it", "ship it") matching anywhere. The affirmative length/position restriction could add friction to longer approval messages ("yes please, and also update the CRM afterwards"), again fail-safe. No client-email risk: the change tightens the external-send gate and touches nothing sponsor-facing (SponsorPortalMailer/SponsorAssetReminderService untouched); no /api/v1 field or schema changes. Must re-run confirmation_gate_spec plus the agent eval harness (EVAL_DM=1 rake eval:agent — golden cases external_send_gated and gate_negation exercise this gate) before shipping.

title: LLM context compaction can split an assistant tool_calls block from its tool results, producing an invalid transcript
description: summarize_older_context! picks the compaction boundary as `recent_start = non_system.last(KEEP_RECENT_TURNS).first` (agent.rb:1263) with no regard for message roles. KEEP_RECENT_TURNS counts MESSAGES, and tool-heavy runs are mostly assistant-tool_calls/tool pairs, so the boundary routinely lands on a role:"tool" message whose issuing assistant message sits in the older span. That older span is then slice!'d away and replaced with a role:"user" summary (agent.rb:1286-1290), leaving orphan tool messages whose tool_call_id references a call that no longer exists in the transcript. The other two compaction paths get this right: stub_older_tool_results! preserves structure, and remove_oldest_non_system_span! removes whole assistant+tool spans.
failure_or_value: Exactly the longest, most valuable runs (big scheduled sweeps, multi-step research) are the ones that reach compaction. On the next request after a mid-block split, OpenAI-compatible servers typically 400 on a tool message with no preceding tool_calls (or the chat template mis-renders it), so the run dies with stop_reason=provider_error, or the model sees garbled history and re-runs tools / hallucinates. The failure is invisible in review because it only reproduces on long conversations.
fix_sketch: After computing recent_start in summarize_older_context!, advance the boundary past any leading tool-role messages so the kept region never starts mid-block: `recent_start_pos = non_system.index(recent_start); recent_start_pos += 1 while messages[non_system[recent_start_pos]][:role] == "tool"` (i.e. extend older_indexes to swallow the trailing tool results of the split block, keeping them WITH their assistant message in the summarized span) — or equivalently walk recent_start backward to include the whole assistant+tool block in the kept region. Add a spec that builds a transcript whose KEEP_RECENT_TURNS boundary lands on a tool message and asserts every remaining tool message has its assistant tool_calls partner.

verdict.reason: Re-read /Users/brianderario/Projects/kerrihq-rails/app/services/ask_savant/agent.rb and the claim survives every refutation attempt. (1) agent.rb:1263 picks the kept-region start as `non_system.last(KEEP_RECENT_TURNS).first` with zero role awareness; KEEP_RECENT_TURNS (line 85, default 20) counts raw messages, and tool-heavy transcripts are built as assistant(tool_calls) followed by one tool message per call (run_loop lines 358, 417, 441), so the boundary routinely lands on a role:"tool" message. Concrete input on the real code path: [system, user] + 12 blocks of [assistant(2 parallel tool_calls), tool, tool] gives 37 non-system messages; non_system.last(20).first is element 17, the first tool message of block 6. summarize_older_context! then slice!s indexes 0..16 (agent.rb:1286), deleting the assistant message that issued those calls, and inserts a role:"user" summary (1287-1290), leaving the transcript [system, "[Earlier conversation summary]", tool(orphan), tool(orphan), ...] where the tool messages' tool_call_id references nothing. (2) That exact array is sent verbatim to OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions (ollama_client.rb:176-182); nothing repairs it downstream — stub_older_tool_results! only rewrites content, and prune_oldest_context! only runs when still over budget. (3) The contrast the finding draws is real: remove_oldest_non_system_span! (1336-1351) explicitly walks assistant+tool blocks as a unit, proving the codebase knows the invariant; summarize_older_context! is the one compaction path that violates it. (4) No existing spec covers it: spec/services/ask_savant/token_compaction_spec.rb exercises summarization only on user/assistant-only conversations (lines 95-102, 152-170), so the suite stays green while the bug ships. Severity stays medium, not high: on Ollama (default backend, lenient compat layer) the usual failure is silent — a mis-rendered chat template and a confused model that re-runs tools or hallucinates prior results — rather than a guaranteed 400; strict OpenAI-compatible backends (OLLAMA_BASE_URL is env-swappable, plus ASK_SAVANT_MODEL_FALLBACKS routing) do hard-reject orphan tool messages, killing exactly the long scheduled sweeps that reach compaction. The fix sketch (extend the summarized span to swallow leading orphan tool messages, or walk the boundary back to the block's assistant message, plus an invariant spec) is correct and matches the existing remove_oldest_non_system_span! pattern.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is a boundary adjustment inside one private method of the AskSavant agent; it touches no API response fields, no DB schema, and nothing near client email (touches_client_email=false — compaction is purely an internal LLM-transcript concern). Two things to watch when shipping: (a) after moving the boundary, re-check the MIN_TURNS_TO_COMPACT guards so a degenerate transcript (long run of consecutive tool messages at the boundary) cannot make older_indexes empty or the adjustment loop run past the array end; (b) the summarized span grows slightly when it swallows trailing tool results, marginally changing what the summary covers — behaviorally invisible. Existing token_compaction_spec expectations are unaffected since none place a tool message at the summarize boundary; add the proposed invariant spec (every remaining role:"tool" message has a preceding assistant tool_calls partner with matching id) to lock it in.

title: Upgrade: top-level crash guard + 'crashed' stop reason in Agent#respond
description: Agent#respond rescues only OllamaClient::Error (agent.rb:288-295). Any StandardError raised by the loop machinery itself — argument parsing (finding 1), compaction slicing, telemetry, TaskNotes parsing in ensure_draft_filed's callers, a future refactor bug — escapes the highest-traffic subsystem entirely. The in-app controller (ask_savant_controller.rb:22) has no rescue, so Brian's phone gets a raw 500; the Slack processor falls to a generic outer rescue with no run telemetry; scheduled runs record a failure with no stop_reason.
failure_or_value: Value: the copilot can never return a raw 500 to Brian, every run — including crashed ones — emits its one-line [AskSavant][telemetry] record with a stable stop_reason, and regressions in the agent harness show up as a countable 'crashed' stop reason instead of scattered stack traces. This is the safety-rail that turns every future harness bug from an outage into a logged, user-visible-but-graceful degradation.
fix_sketch: In Agent#respond add a final `rescue StandardError => e` mirroring the OllamaClient::Error branch: log e.class/e.message/top backtrace frames, telemetry.finish(stop_reason: "crashed"), log_telemetry, notify @observer, and return Result.new(text: "I hit an internal error partway through that. What I'd already done is saved; try again or rephrase.", tools_used: Array(@tools_used).uniq, error: e.message, delivered_actions: Array(@delivery_actions).uniq, telemetry: telemetry). Add "crashed" to RunTelemetry::STOP_REASONS (additive vocabulary, run_telemetry.rb:28). No caller changes needed.

verdict.reason: Confirmed as a real, feasible, not-yet-existing upgrade. Agent#respond rescues only OllamaClient::Error (agent.rb:288); AskSavantController#create has no rescue and ApplicationController only rescues Pundit::NotAuthorizedError, so any other StandardError escaping the agent 500s the in-app copilot; the Slack processor's generic rescue (event_processor.rb:75) loses all run telemetry; ScheduledAgentRunJob's own comment (scheduled_agent_run_job.rb:88-89) admits result is nil when respond raises, so crashed scheduled runs persist no stop_reason. "crashed" is absent from STOP_REASONS and nothing validates against that list, so adding it is purely additive. The fix sketch is sound (telemetry helper is ||=-safe, Array(@tools_used) nil-safe, callers already branch on result.error). Downgraded from high to medium because the finding overstates the crash surface: parse_arguments already returns :invalid_json on bad JSON, ensure_draft_filed already has its own StandardError rescue (agent.rb:877), and ToolExecutor#invoke_tool_handler globally rescues all tool-handler crashes (tool_executor.rb:250). The genuinely unguarded paths are narrower — StandingOrdersContext.call (no rescue), the compaction/stub/prune machinery, telemetry/response-shape handling, and future refactor bugs — and I found no concrete input that crashes today's code. Valuable safety rail, not a live outage.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. touches_client_email=false: a crash guard sends nothing and is nowhere near sponsor mail. API-compat is clean: Result struct fields unchanged, "crashed" is a new additive stop_reason value that no consumer validates against a whitelist (flow_executor.rb:192 and scheduled_run_failure_alert_job.rb:120 just stringify). Two things to watch: (1) ScheduledAgentRunJob currently re-raises on a crash (line 91), surfacing it to Solid Queue's failure/retry semantics; after the guard, a crashed run returns a Result with error set, so the run is marked :failed and ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob fires, but the job no longer raises — queue-level retry for crashes goes away (this matches how provider_error behaves today, but it is a semantics change worth a spec). (2) A blanket rescue StandardError can mask coding bugs as soft failures in dev/eval; mitigate by logging e.class, message, and top backtrace frames in the rescue and keeping error populated on the Result so the eval harness and AgentRun rows still count these as failures. Guard tests: assert the OllamaClient::Error branch still wins for provider errors (it is more specific and listed first), and that the new branch does not swallow ensure_draft_filed's already-rescued path twice.

title: Post-answer false-claim grounding ignores the deadline and can hang an interactive request for up to 180 extra seconds
description: ground_false_code_nonexecution_claim is invoked in the respond tail (agent.rb:270) and inside run_loop with NO past_deadline? guard, unlike its sibling direct_forced_code_tool_result which is gated on !past_deadline?. When the final text matches CODE_FALSE_NONEXECUTION_HINT and contains a PR number, checked_code_status_from_claim (agent.rb:1023-1032) synchronously executes check_pull_request with wait_seconds=FORCED_CODE_CHECK_WAIT_SECONDS (180), which polls GitHub CI for up to 3 minutes.
failure_or_value: On the :app surface the user is waiting in the browser with a 240s run budget. A coding conversation that ends at ~t=235s with text like 'there is no PR #57' triggers a further 180s blocking GitHub poll — total request time up to ~420s, past typical proxy/HTTP timeouts on Render, so Brian sees a dead request even though an answer existed. It also burns worker time after the run has already declared itself out of budget.
fix_sketch: In ground_false_code_nonexecution_claim (or at its call sites), skip checked_code_status_from_claim when past_deadline?; when not past deadline, clamp the wait to remaining budget: `wait = [[(@deadline - monotonic).to_i - 5, FORCED_CODE_CHECK_WAIT_SECONDS].min, 0].max` and pass that as wait_seconds (0 = single status read, still grounds the claim without polling). Tool-evidence grounding (grounded_code_status_from_tool_evidence) is local and stays unconditional.

verdict.reason: Re-read the actual code: ground_false_code_nonexecution_claim is invoked un-gated at agent.rb:270 and agent.rb:382 while its sibling direct_forced_code_tool_result is deadline-gated at :377 and :658, proving the omission. checked_code_status_from_claim (agent.rb:1023-1032) passes wait_seconds=180 to check_pull_request, which reaches CodeShippingClient#pull_request_status (code_shipping_client.rb:65-78) — a sleep(10) poll loop that blocks up to the full wait while CI is pending. Concrete reproducing inputs on the real path: in-app copilot (ask_savant_controller.rb:22 runs respond synchronously, :app surface = 240s budget), user message containing e.g. "check PR #57 and merge if green" (satisfies the broad coding_requested? regex at agent.rb:755), run exhausts its budget in tool calls and exits via wrap_up (agent.rb:360-362), wrap-up text like "I never actually called check_pull_request, so I can't confirm PR #57" matches CODE_FALSE_NONEXECUTION_HINT and contains a PR number, no check/ship tool result exists in this run's messages so tool-evidence grounding returns nil, PR #57 exists with pending CI — the request then blocks up to 180 further seconds (~420s total) inside a synchronous HTTP request with no rack-timeout. Kept at medium because the trigger requires several regex conditions plus pending CI to align, and the Slack surface (900s budget) degrades rather than dies.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix only clamps an internal wait_seconds value passed to check_pull_request in a post-answer grounding tail: no /api/v1 field renames or removals, no DB schema change, and nothing near sponsor/client email (touches_client_email=false). Behavior change to watch: when grounding fires past the deadline, a wait of 0 does a single status read and may report CI as "pending" instead of a definitive pass/fail — a slightly less conclusive but still truthful grounded answer. Keep grounded_code_status_from_tool_evidence unconditional (it is local and instant), and only clamp/skip the GitHub-polling fallback, or the anti-hallucination grounding gets weaker than today. Add a spec pinning the clamped wait so a future refactor does not restore the unbounded 180s poll.

title: Forced merge/check scrapes the PR number from loose text and can act on the wrong (green Kerri) PR
description: When the anti-stall harness force-executes merge_pull_request (bypassing the confirmation gate via forced:true), it resolves the PR number with pull_number_from_messages (agent.rb:946-960), which walks ALL messages newest-first and returns the FIRST thing matching `\bPR\s*#?(\d+)\b` or a github pull URL — including numbers in the model's own prose ('this is similar to what PR #233 did') and in unrelated tool results — before ever consulting the user's actual instruction. DEPLOY_EXISTING_PR_REQUEST_HINT ('deploy it now') doesn't capture a number at all, so 'it' is resolved purely by recency of any PR-shaped string.
failure_or_value: Brian says 'deploy it now' after a session that discussed two PRs (the new fix #250 and a referenced older #233). If the most recent PR-number mention in the transcript is #233, the harness force-merges #233. CodeShippingClient limits blast (kerri/ branch + CI green required, code_shipping_client.rb:109-122, 356-359), but merging a different green Kerri PR than intended still deploys unreviewed-for-this-moment code to production with the confirmation gate bypassed.
fix_sketch: Tighten resolution order in direct_merge_pull_request_result/direct_check_pull_request_result: (1) if the user's latest message contains an explicit number (extend DEPLOYMENT_BOUNDARY_REQUEST_HINT to capture it), use exactly that; (2) otherwise use latest_code_tool_result(messages, CODE_MUTATION_TOOLS) — the PR this run actually opened/revised — via pull_number_from_result; (3) only fall back to the free-text scan when neither exists, and for merge specifically, refuse the forced path in that case (return nil so the normal prompt-based flow asks). Log which source resolved the number in the existing forced-tool warn line.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every link: agent.rb:377 routes any plain-text model turn into direct_forced_code_tool_result; "deploy it now" matches DEPLOY_EXISTING_PR_REQUEST_HINT (line 131, no digit capture) and deployment_requested? (1138-1141) is satisfied by the same loose transcript scan it later merges from. direct_merge_pull_request_result (918) resolves the PR as pull_number_from_messages FIRST and the user's own message LAST; pull_number_from_messages (946-960) walks all roles newest-first matching \bPR\s*#?(\d+)\b, so assistant prose appended after the real ship_code result ("this follows PR #233") or a JSON tool result whose body text mentions a PR (falls through to pull_number_from_text on the raw JSON at line 953) wins over the actual shipped PR. execute_direct_tool (936) passes forced:true, which tool_executor.rb:198-228 uses to bypass the confirmation gate. Concrete input: transcript = [user "fix X", ship_code result w/ pull/250, assistant prose citing PR #233, user "deploy it now", model plain-text stall] → forced merge_pull_request(pull_number:"233"). It is actually worse than claimed: line 784 short-circuits on deployment_requested?, so even a clarifying question from the model ("which PR, #250 or #233?") is discarded and the harness merges the most recent transcript mention; and an explicit user number can also lose since latest_human_user_content is the last fallback. Specs (agent_spec.rb:1051-1136) only cover single-PR transcripts, so nothing guards this. Severity stays medium, not high, because code_shipping_client.rb:111-123 + ensure_kerri_code_shipping_pr! (356-359) require open + kerri/ branch + body marker + CI green, so the wrong target must itself be another open green Kerri PR — but stacked Kerri PRs are this shop's normal state and merge = production deploy.
verdict.ship_risk: Low blast radius: the fix touches only the internal AskSavant anti-stall harness (agent.rb private methods), no /api/v1 fields, no DB schema, and touches_client_email=false — nothing near sponsor-facing mail. Main regression risk is over-tightening the resolution order so the forced-merge path stops firing for the legitimate single-PR "deploy it now" cases it was built for (the run-to-completion stall fix); the existing specs at spec/services/ask_savant/agent_spec.rb:1051-1136 pin that behavior and must stay green, and new two-PR-transcript specs should be added. Preferring the user's explicit number and this run's CODE_MUTATION_TOOLS result, and refusing the forced path (returning nil so the normal prompt-based flow asks) only when neither exists, keeps current tests passing. Logging the resolution source in the existing warn line is pure observability. No client email or API backward-compat exposure.

title: Upgrade: expose per-tool circuit-breaker state in agent_runtime_status / runtime health
description: ToolCircuitBreaker keeps open/half-open state per org+tool in Rails.cache, but nothing can enumerate or report it: when the breaker opens (5 transient/bug failures in 10 min) every external tool call for 5 minutes returns 'temporarily disabled after repeated failures', and the only trace is per-run tool errors buried in logs. agent_runtime_status (tool_executor.rb:3931-3935) — the tool Brian is told to use for 'is Kerri healthy / stuck' — returns AgentRuntimeHealth.snapshot with no breaker visibility.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: when Graph mail or Apollo is flapping, scheduled sweeps silently degrade for whole runs and Brian's 'is Kerri healthy?' question in Slack answers 'all good'. With breaker state surfaced, the agent (and the QUEUE badge / task_queue_health path already used for diagnosis) can answer 'search_mail circuit is open, retrying in 240s' — turning a mystery no-op run into a named, time-bounded incident. Purely additive JSON, no schema or API renames.
fix_sketch: Add ToolCircuitBreaker#snapshot: iterate ToolExecutor::EXTERNAL_TOOLS (the full key space is known), read each cache key, and return entries where state != closed as [{ tool:, state:, retry_after_seconds:, failures: }]. Merge it into AgentRuntimeHealth.snapshot as an additive `circuit_breakers` array (and optionally into GET /api/v1/task_queue_health the same way). agent_runtime_status then reports it for free; add one line to the system prompt's runtime-status guidance if desired.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim: ToolCircuitBreaker (app/services/ask_savant/tool_circuit_breaker.rb) exposes only blocked_for_seconds/record_failure!/record_success! with state in Rails.cache keys tool_breaker:{org_id}:{tool_name}; nothing in the codebase enumerates or reports it (rg for circuit_open/tool_breaker hits only tool_executor.rb and agent.rb per-run error-category telemetry). AgentRuntimeHealth.snapshot (app/services/agent_runtime_health.rb:12-23) has no breaker section, yet agent_runtime_status (tool_executor.rb:3931-3934) and GET /api/v1/agent_runtime_health return it verbatim, and system_prompt.rb:52 directs the agent to use it for is-Kerri-healthy questions. When the breaker opens (5 failures/10 min -> 5 min open, tool_executor.rb:215-221 returns category circuit_open per call), scheduled runs degrade with no aggregate visibility. Fix is feasible: EXTERNAL_TOOLS (tool_executor.rb:171-186) is a frozen known key space, so a read-only snapshot via read_multi is one cache query. One caveat: the snapshot must NOT call blocked_for_seconds, which mutates state (open->half_open write at breaker line 50); it needs a pure read path.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Purely additive JSON key (circuit_breakers) in AgentRuntimeHealth.snapshot; no existing field renamed/removed, so the round-the-clock /api/v1 agent pollers are unaffected. No DB migration. Zero client-email surface (touches_client_email=false): breaker state is internal diagnostics only. Two things to get right: (1) the snapshot path must be read-only on the cache -- reusing blocked_for_seconds would flip open breakers to half_open as a side effect of every health poll, effectively letting probes through early; (2) keep the array empty-by-default and org-scoped (keys already include org id) so the unscoped snapshot (organization: nil) either skips breakers or iterates orgs explicitly. Cost is ~30 cache reads (one read_multi) per health call, negligible on Solid Cache.

title: Upgrade: make tool-result digestion and compaction summarization deadline-aware
description: prepared_tool_content (agent.rb:465-479) synchronously calls the balanced model (max_tokens 4096) for every research_web/browser_run/read_mail_thread result over 12KB, and generate_compaction_summary (agent.rb:1296-1317) synchronously calls the fast model, regardless of how much run budget remains. Neither consults past_deadline? or the remaining seconds, so a run at t=230s of a 240s interactive budget still launches a multi-ten-second secondary LLM call whose output it will never get to use (the very next deadline check triggers wrap-up).
failure_or_value: Concrete value: faster interactive turns on Brian's phone — the :app surface is where he waits live, and each large tool result currently costs an extra synchronous condense round-trip even when the turn is about to be cut off. Skipping digestion under deadline pressure (falling back to the existing truncate_json path, which is already the fail-open behavior when the condense call errors) trims dead-weight latency at exactly the moment the run can least afford it, with zero behavior change on runs that have budget.
fix_sketch: Add a helper `remaining_budget = @deadline - monotonic`. In prepared_tool_content, `return json if remaining_budget < 45` before calling condense_tool_result. In summarize_older_context!, skip the LLM summary (fall straight through to stub/prune, which compact_context! already does next) when remaining_budget < 30 — pruning is instant and the stub path preserves tool names. Record a telemetry nudge/counter (e.g. record_nudge(kind: "digest_skipped_deadline")) so the skip rate is observable.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms both mechanics: prepared_tool_content (agent.rb:465-479) synchronously calls the balanced model (max_tokens 4096) for any research_web/browser_run/read_mail_thread result over 12KB with zero deadline awareness, and generate_compaction_summary (agent.rb:1296-1313) synchronously calls the fast model from compact_context! at the top of every iteration, also deadline-blind. past_deadline? appears only at lines 360/377/388/413/658/665/840 — never in the digestion or compaction-summary paths. Concrete tail case on the :app surface (240s deadline, line 44): a research_web call issued at t=220 finishing at t=245 with a 40KB result still runs the full condense round-trip before line 360 triggers wrap_up, extending Brian's live wait by the condense duration. One correction to the finding: the condensed output is not literally unused — wrap_up (line 622) includes it in the final no-tools request — but its marginal value there vs the existing truncate_json fail-open fallback (lines 476-478) is near zero, so the latency-saving argument survives. The fix is feasible and small: the compaction skip safely falls through to the instant stub/prune path already in compact_context! (1153-1161), and telemetry.record_nudge(kind:) already exists for the observability counter. Severity stays medium: real interactive-latency win but only in the deadline-pressure tail of runs; no correctness bug today.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Entirely internal to the AskSavant agent loop: no /api/v1 field changes, no DB migration, no mailer or sponsor-facing path (touches_client_email=false). Behavior changes only in the final seconds of a run's budget; the skip paths reuse existing fail-open fallbacks (truncate_json for digestion, stub/prune for compaction). Two watch items: (1) tune the cutoff as remaining-seconds, not a fraction, so the 900s slack surface and 150s subagent budgets both behave sensibly — a too-large cutoff would silently disable digestion for subagents whose whole budget is 150s; (2) skipping the compaction summary near deadline means the wrap-up request may carry a stubbed/pruned (lossier) context, marginally degrading the final status message quality in rare long runs. Per house rules, run EVAL_DM=1 rake eval:agent plus the full suite before shipping since this touches the agent prompt/loop path.

title: Socket Mode connection has no liveness detection — a silently dead socket makes the bot deaf until restart
description: The read loop is `until @closed { driver.parse(io.readpartial(READ_CHUNK_BYTES)) }` with no read deadline and no tracking of Slack's ping frames. If the TCP connection dies without a FIN/RST (NAT timeout, network partition, Render network blip), readpartial blocks forever, the workspace thread never raises, and SocketModeRunner's reconnect loop never fires. Additionally, Slack's Socket Mode `{"type":"disconnect","reason":"refresh_requested"}` envelope (sent before Slack retires a connection, roughly every few hours) is not handled — handle_envelope treats it as 'not events_api' and just acks, relying entirely on Slack's close frame arriving intact.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: Kerri/Oliver stop answering Slack silently and stay deaf indefinitely (Brian on his phone sees no reply at all, no error) until someone restarts the socket worker. A read deadline turns every dead-socket scenario into an automatic reconnect within ~90 seconds instead of a human-noticed outage.
fix_sketch: In SocketModeConnection#run, track `last_read_at = Time.current` after each successful readpartial, and replace the blocking read with a select-with-timeout: `readable = IO.select([io.to_io], nil, nil, 15)` (expose the underlying SSL socket via a WebSocketIo#to_io method; also drain `@socket.pending`-buffered bytes first for OpenSSL). If no data for e.g. 90 seconds (Slack pings every ~30s, so 3 missed pings), `raise Error, "socket silent for 90s"` so the runner's reconnect loop takes over. In handle_envelope, when `envelope["type"] == "disconnect"`, set `@closed = true` (and close the io) to reconnect proactively instead of waiting on Slack's close frame. Add a spec that a silent socket raises after the deadline.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim. (1) app/services/slack/socket_mode_connection.rb:48-50 is exactly `until @closed { driver.parse(io.readpartial(READ_CHUNK_BYTES)) }`; WebSocketIo#readpartial (line 138-140) delegates straight to OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#readpartial with no deadline, and connect (lines 124-132) never sets SO_KEEPALIVE, so a half-open TCP connection (NAT timeout, Slack LB failover without RST, Render network partition) blocks readpartial forever without raising. (2) The runner's reconnect loop (socket_mode_runner.rb:48-60) only fires on a raised exception, so it never triggers on a silent hang; bin/render-worker runs this in a single thread on Render with no external watchdog, health check, or restart cron (grep found no ping/pong tracking, no IO.select, no liveness anywhere in app/services/slack). The bot writes nothing while idle (acks only follow received envelopes), so no EPIPE would surface either — the deaf state is genuinely indefinite until a human restarts the worker. (3) handle_envelope (lines 60-63) treats a Slack `{"type":"disconnect"}` envelope as not-events_api and just acks (a no-op since disconnect envelopes carry no envelope_id), relying entirely on Slack's subsequent close frame/FIN arriving intact — accurate, though this half is secondary since the FIN usually does arrive. websocket-driver only auto-pongs during parse, i.e. only when bytes arrive, so it provides no liveness. The comment at line 15 shows the authors know Slack pings regularly, which makes a ~90s read deadline both safe and effective. High-value: Kerri/Oliver in Slack are Brian's primary phone interface and the failure mode is invisible to a non-technical user.
verdict.ship_risk: Low and contained: the change is inside SocketModeConnection only — no client email (touches_client_email=false), no /api/v1 surface, no DB schema. Two implementation pitfalls to watch: (a) IO.select on an OpenSSL socket must drain @socket.pending-buffered bytes before selecting (or use read_nonblock with IO::WaitReadable), otherwise data already decrypted into the SSL buffer can sit unread until the deadline falsely fires; (b) too short a deadline causes reconnect churn — 90s (3 missed ~30s Slack pings) is safe, and each spurious reconnect is self-healing anyway since the runner reconnects with backoff. Worst realistic regression is an occasional extra reconnect, versus the current worst case of an indefinite silent outage.

title: Messages from OTHER bots are attributed to the agent itself as assistant turns in conversation history
description: bot_message?(message, workspace) returns true for ANY message with `bot_id` present, not just this workspace's own bot (`message["bot_id"].present? || user == workspace.bot_user_id`). conversation_history then assigns those turns `role: "assistant"` (line 245-246). The spec suite only covers the own-bot case (event_processor_attribution_spec.rb uses bot_id equal to the workspace bot).
failure_or_value: Kerri and Oliver (two installs, same Slack team) share a channel like #kerri-jam. A user mentions @Kerri in a thread where Oliver has replied: Oliver's messages arrive in Kerri's history as Kerri's OWN prior assistant turns. Kerri then 'remembers saying' things it never said — it will defend, extend, or contradict Oliver's answer as if it were its own, and the human-speaker attribution work (the multi_speaker naming added after the 2026-07-03 #kerri-jam confusion) silently excludes other bots from human_senders too, so they get no speaker label either. Same failure for any workflow/webhook bot posting in the channel (GitHub, Reclaim, etc.): its output is absorbed as the agent's own words.
fix_sketch: Split bot_message? into own_bot_message? (user == workspace.bot_user_id, or bot_id matches a stored own-bot id — capture the workspace's bot_id once via auth.test or from its own posted messages) and foreign_bot_message?. In conversation_history: own bot => role assistant (unchanged); foreign bot => role user with a speaker prefix from the message's `username`/`bot_profile.name` (e.g. "GitHub (bot): ..."). Keep the history-attachment exclusion keyed on own-bot only. Add a spec: thread with own-bot + foreign-bot messages asserts foreign bot lands as a labeled user turn.

verdict.reason: bot_message? (event_processor.rb:335-338) returns true for ANY message with bot_id present, and conversation_history (lines 245-246) maps every such message to role "assistant", so a foreign bot's turn (Oliver, GitHub, Reclaim, workflow bots) is rebuilt as the agent's own prior reply. The multi-install-same-team setup is documented in the code itself (configuration.rb:131-134: "several installs (Kerri, Oliver, Hardware FYI)"), and history_messages fetches the full thread regardless of author, so the failing input is concrete: thread_messages returning {"bot_id" => "BOLIVER", "subtype" => "bot_message", ...} produces an assistant turn in Kerri's history. Foreign bots are also excluded from human_senders (line 220) so they get no speaker label, and their attachments are dropped (line 290). Specs only cover the own-bot case (attribution_spec.rb:66 uses bot_id equal to the workspace bot). Medium is right: it corrupts agent context and can cause visibly wrong behavior in shared channels, but only when another bot has posted in the same thread/DM, and it never sends anything externally.
verdict.ship_risk: Low blast radius: the fix touches only internal history reconstruction, no /api/v1 fields, no DB schema, no client email (touches_client_email=false). Main regression risk is own-bot detection: if the workspace's own posted messages ever lack the "user" field (e.g. webhook-posted or misconfigured bot_user_id), an own-bot check keyed only on user id would flip Kerri's own prior replies from assistant to labeled user turns, breaking follow-up flows like "execute this PR" that depend on the agent seeing its own proposal as an assistant turn. Mitigate by matching own bot_id too (capture via auth.test or from a posted message) and adding both an own-bot and foreign-bot spec. Also keep the line-229 subtype gate consistent so foreign bot_message-subtype turns become labeled user turns rather than being dropped, or history in bot-heavy channels shrinks unexpectedly.

title: accept_bot_messages workspaces can never actually be answered: EventProcessor drops every bot event that WorkspacePolicy approved
description: The pipeline has a full bot-to-bot feature: Configuration exposes `accept_bot_messages`, WorkspacePolicy#bot_decision allows bot events when it's on, and BotLoopGuard exists solely to rate-limit them. But EventProcessor#actionable_event? line 94 unconditionally returns false when `@event["bot_id"].present?`. So for an accept_bot_messages workspace, every bot message passes policy, gets an AgentSession + queued AgentTask, is picked up by SlackAgentTaskJob, and then EventProcessor returns :ignored — the task is finalized `succeeded (outcome: ignored)` and no reply is ever posted.
failure_or_value: Configure a workspace with accept_bot_messages: true so another agent (e.g. the Kerri bot identity relaying to OpenClaw agents) can talk to Savant: the sender bot posts, a task is created and 'succeeds', and nothing ever replies. The feature is a silent no-op end to end, plus it manufactures junk succeeded-task rows (one per inbound bot message, up to BotLoopGuard's 20/min) that pollute task metrics.
fix_sketch: Thread the workspace's accept_bot_messages? into EventProcessor#actionable_event?: allow bot events when the resolved workspace has accept_bot_messages? AND the event's bot_id is not the workspace's own bot (loop safety), e.g. move the bot_id check after resolved_workspace and make it `return false if @event["bot_id"].present? && !resolved_workspace&.accept_bot_messages?`. UserResolver must then handle a bot sender (no `user` field): fall back to default_user_email explicitly for bot-authored events. Add specs for an accept_bot_messages workspace getting a reply and for the own-bot self-loop still being ignored. If instead the feature is intentionally retired, delete accept_bot_messages/bot_decision/BotLoopGuard so the config can't lie.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every link in the chain: WorkspacePolicy#decision_for (workspace_policy.rb:17,49-54) allows bot events when accept_bot_messages is true (checked before the subtype filter and reply-policy switch, gated only by BotLoopGuard), SessionQueue (session_queue.rb:22-35) then persists an AgentSession + queued AgentTask and schedules SlackAgentTaskJob, which calls EventProcessor (slack_agent_task_job.rb:31). EventProcessor#actionable_event? line 94 unconditionally returns false on @event["bot_id"].present?, so call returns :ignored and finalize_task! marks the task succeeded (outcome: ignored) with no reply ever posted. Concrete input: any workspace config with accept_bot_messages: true plus an event_callback carrying event.bot_id — task created, "succeeds", silence. EventProcessor is the only consumer of these payloads (both call sites are in SlackAgentTaskJob), so there is no alternate bot-handling path; accept_bot_messages, bot_decision, and the entire BotLoopGuard class serve events that are always dropped. UserResolver already falls back to default_user_email for a nil sender, so the sketched fix is feasible. Severity stays medium not high because no config in the repo enables the flag today (docs example shows false), so it is a confirmed dead feature / silent trap plus junk succeeded-task manufacture, not an active outage.
verdict.ship_risk: Moderate if fixed, near-zero if the feature is deleted. The fix touches actionable_event?, the hot gate for ALL inbound Slack events (every Kerri/Oliver DM and mention), so a regression could either drop human messages or, worse, let the bot react to its own posts: own-bot exclusion is mandatory since BotLoopGuard only caps a self-loop at 20 msgs/min/channel, it does not prevent one. The finding's sketch is also incomplete in two ways a shipper must cover: (1) line 98's subtype filter still drops subtype:"bot_message" (how most bot posts arrive), so the subtype gate needs the same accept_bot_messages carve-out WorkspacePolicy already has; (2) conversation_history's bot_message? (event_processor.rb:229,245) maps every bot message to role "assistant", so a foreign bot's turns would be misattributed as Kerri's own replies — needs own-bot vs foreign-bot distinction. No client-email exposure (Slack-internal only, mailers untouched) and no /api/v1 or DB schema changes required; task output values stay additive. Alternative low-risk ship: retire the flag path (config field, bot_decision, BotLoopGuard) so the config cannot lie, at the cost of the bot-to-bot relay capability the kerri-bot use case may eventually want.

title: default_user_email fallback lets any unmapped Slack workspace member or guest act as Brian
description: UserResolver tries (1) the configured slack-id→email map, (2) the Slack profile email, then (3) `workspace.default_user_email` — which in the KerriHQ installs is brian@kerrihq.com. Steps 1 and 2 only win if they resolve to a User who is a member of the org; anyone else falls through to step 3 and is resolved AS the default user. There is no check that the falling-through Slack account belongs to a trusted person.
failure_or_value: A single-channel guest or new hire added to the Slack workspace (contractor, S&W collaborator, event vendor) DMs the Kerri app. Their profile email matches no Savant user, so they resolve to Brian's User and the agent runs with Brian's full capability set: reading Brian's mailboxes via the Superhuman/Graph tools, CRM deals, the company brain, Granola transcripts — all of which are gated 'Brian-only' by resolved identity. The reply also goes straight back to the guest's DM.
fix_sketch: Constrain the fallback in UserResolver#resolve: only use default_user_email when the Slack user id appears in workspace.user_email_by_slack_id, OR when the Slack profile email's domain is on an allowlist derived from the org (e.g. domains of existing member emails / a new `trusted_domains` workspace config key — additive config, existing installs unchanged if you default trusted_domains to the domains already present in user_email_by_slack_id). When the fallback is refused, EventProcessor already posts the clean 'I need this Slack user mapped...' setup error, which is the right UX. Log the refused slack_user_id for easy mapping. Add specs: unmapped external-domain user gets nil; mapped user still falls back.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms the exact mechanics: UserResolver#resolve (app/services/slack/user_resolver.rb:12-24) tries config map, then Slack profile email, then workspace.default_user_email, returning the first email that maps to an org-member User — with zero check on who the sending Slack account is. Concrete input: any workspace guest/new member/Slack Connect user whose profile email has no Savant User row (e.g. guest@vendor.com) DMs or mentions the bot; steps 1-2 miss, step 3 resolves them AS brian@kerrihq.com. EventProcessor then runs AskSavant::Agent with user=Brian (event_processor.rb:47-63), and every downstream gate keys off that resolved email: superhuman_email? (tool_executor.rb:2518, S&W mailbox), granola_email? (:2527), full_member_of? brain/CRM gates (:415, :803). The reply goes back to the guest's DM, and the audit run records initiated_by=brian@kerrihq.com, hiding the impersonation. No compensating control exists: WorkspacePolicy gates only channels/reply-policy/bot-loops, never sender identity; the access_groups config key is parsed (configuration.rb:33,235) but referenced nowhere else — dead config; no user_resolver_spec pins the open fallback as intended. Severity stays high (not critical) because exploitation requires presence in the Slack workspace of a 3-person company — but guests, S&W collaborators in shared channels, and Slack Connect are all realistic in this org.
verdict.ship_risk: Low-to-medium, with one trap: some installs likely carry an empty or sparse user_email_by_slack_id and depend on the default_user_email fallback for Brian's own DMs (that is plainly why the fallback exists — the Oliver/HWFYI secondary installs in specs configure only default_user_email). Deriving trusted_domains purely from the slack-id map would yield an empty allowlist and lock Brian out of his own bot until IDs are mapped. Mitigate by also trusting domains of existing org-member emails, or shipping a log-only warn mode for a few days before enforcing, and verifying each prod install's map first. The refusal path already exists (post_setup_error at event_processor.rb:48) so failure UX is clean. touches_client_email=false — no sponsor-facing send anywhere near this path; no /api/v1 field renames; additive config key only, no schema change. Scheduled runs (scheduled_agent_run_job.rb) resolve Slack targets from email→slack_id, the reverse direction, so they are unaffected.

title: First-ever concurrent events race on session/task creation and SlackEventJob has no retry — the losing Slack message is dropped with no reply
description: find_or_update_session does find_or_initialize_by(session_key:) + save!, and agent_sessions.session_key has a unique index (db/schema.rb:326). Two messages sent quickly into a brand-new conversation are enqueued as two SlackEventJobs; both workers find no session, both save!, one raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique. ApplicationJob defines no retry_on (both commented out) and SlackEventJob adds none, so the failing job lands in Solid Queue's failed set permanently — that Slack message never becomes a task and never gets a reply. The same unguarded pattern exists for AgentTask (source, source_ref) unique index (schema.rb:384) on Slack's redelivery of the same event to two workers, and in AmbientEventRecorder (which additionally has a read-modify-write race on metadata ambient_history that silently drops entries).
failure_or_value: Brian opens a fresh DM with a new install (or the first message after a session-key change) and fires two messages back to back: message #2's job dies with RecordNotUnique, no task, no reply, no error surfaced in Slack — it looks like the bot ignored him. Any transient DB deadlock in enqueue has the same silent-drop effect.
fix_sketch: Two-line hardening plus a rescue: (1) In SlackEventJob add `retry_on ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, ActiveRecord::Deadlocked, wait: 2.seconds, attempts: 3` — the whole enqueue path is idempotent (find_or_initialize on unique keys), so a retry converges to find-and-update. (2) Optionally rescue RecordNotUnique inside find_or_update_session / find_or_create_task and retry the find once, so the common case doesn't even burn a job retry. Add a spec simulating the unique violation and asserting the event still produces a task.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim. The slack Solid Queue worker runs threads: 2 (config/queue.yml), so two SlackEventJobs execute concurrently. find_or_update_session (session_queue.rb:50-62) is find_or_initialize_by + save! against a unique index on agent_sessions.session_key (schema.rb:326) with no lock and no rescue; a model-level uniqueness validation exists but races identically, so the loser raises RecordNotUnique or RecordInvalid. SlackEventJob and ApplicationJob define zero retry_on (both commented out), and the only recovery machinery, Slack::SessionRecovery, exclusively inspects SlackAgentTaskJob rows for an existing AgentTask (session_recovery.rb:201-205) — a dead SlackEventJob has no task yet, so nothing ever retries it: the Slack message is silently dropped with no reply. Concrete input: two events sharing a brand-new session_key (first two messages of a new channel thread or fresh DM; every new thread mints a new key per event_context.rb:94-96) landing within the ~100ms pickup window, or any transient DB deadlock during enqueue. Minor corrections: the AgentTask (source, source_ref) race is largely benign for the user (the winner still creates and schedules the task; note the socket-mode path at socket_mode_connection.rb:27 has no event dedupe unlike the webhook controller), and the AmbientEventRecorder ambient_history last-writer-wins race (ambient_event_recorder.rb:30-39) is real but only loses a context line. The fix (retry_on RecordNotUnique/Deadlocked in SlackEventJob plus a rescue-and-refind in find_or_update_session) is correct because the entire enqueue path is idempotent, and mirrors existing patterns in the codebase (agent_memory_store.rb:59, several retry_on jobs). Severity stays medium: trigger frequency is low, but the failure is a silent, unrecoverable drop on Brian's primary agent surface with zero observability, and the retry hardening also covers all transient DB errors on this path.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is a job-level retry_on plus an optional rescue-and-refind inside SessionQueue — no schema change, no API field changes, no client-email surface (touches_client_email=false). The enqueue path is idempotent (session find-or-init on unique key, task dedup by event_id), so a retry converges rather than double-creating; the one thing to watch is that retrying a job whose first attempt partially succeeded (task saved, append_event! failed) re-finds the persisted task and returns early, which is correct. Broad retry_on RecordNotUnique could theoretically mask a future non-idempotent bug in this job, so cap attempts at 2-3 and keep the failed-set visible. Fixing the AmbientEventRecorder history race properly needs a row lock or JSONB append, slightly more blast radius — fine to defer. Add a spec simulating the unique violation to lock the behavior in.

title: Progress draft message is left behind above every answer — delete it after the final reply posts (phone UX)
description: For every agent turn with progress_mode on, ProgressDraft posts a 'Working: Using `tool`' message and finally edits it to 'Done: Posting the result now.' — then the real answer posts as a separate message and the Done message sits there forever. Client has no delete_message, and nothing cleans it up. In a DM on Brian's phone every exchange is: question → stale 'Done' stub → answer, doubling the visual noise and burying answers when scrolling back.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: every Slack conversation gets half as many bot messages; scrollback on mobile reads as clean Q→A pairs. Also removes the misleading permanent 'Blocked' stub duplication on error turns (the error reply already says the same thing).
fix_sketch: Add Client#delete_message(channel:, ts:) calling chat.delete. In EventProcessor#call, after post_reply succeeds (line 71), if @agent_task&.metadata&.dig("progress_message_ts") is present, delete it (rescue Client::Error and log; if delete fails, fall back to the current agent_finished edit) and clear progress_message_ts from task metadata + session progress fields. Keep the 'Blocked' edit path when post_reply itself fails so the user still sees something. The progress events written to agent_task_events (which SessionRecovery#retry_safe? reads) are untouched, so retry safety is unaffected. Specs: successful turn deletes the draft; failed post keeps it.

verdict.reason: Every claim survives re-reading. ProgressDraft (app/services/slack/progress_draft.rb:28-32) edits the progress stub to "Done: Posting the result now." via agent_finished (called from ask_savant/agent.rb:279/286/293), then EventProcessor posts the answer as a separate chat.postMessage (event_processor.rb:71); Client (app/services/slack/client.rb) has no delete_message and a repo-wide search finds no cleanup path for progress_message_ts. progress_mode defaults to "progress" (configuration.rb:230), and in DMs both the stub and the answer post top-level (event_processor.rb:185-194), so Brian's phone scrollback really is question → permanent "Done" stub → answer on every turn. The retry-safety claim also checks out: SessionRecovery#retry_safe? (session_recovery.rb:142-147) reads agent_task_events rows, not the Slack message, so deleting the stub cannot affect retry decisions. The code itself acknowledges users delete these stubs by hand (progress_draft.rb:60-63 comment). Fix is real and additive: add Client#delete_message (chat.delete, same bot token/chat:write scope), delete after post_reply succeeds, keep the "Blocked" edit on failure, and also handle the :cancelled early-return at event_processor.rb:66-69 which currently strands a "Working" stub with no answer.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. No client email involvement (Slack-internal, KMG workspace bots only) and no public-API or DB-schema change: /api/v1 fields untouched, agent_runtime_status keeps its progress_message_ts key (it just becomes null on finished tasks, which is truthful). Residual risks: (1) chat.delete can fail in edge cases (message already user-deleted, rare admin-restricted channels) — must rescue Client::Error and fall back to the existing "Done" edit so a failed delete never fails the turn or masks a successful answer post; (2) delete must run strictly AFTER post_reply succeeds, otherwise a Slack outage between delete and post leaves the user with zero visible response — order of operations is load-bearing; (3) one extra Tier-3 API call per turn, negligible; (4) specs in reply_delivery_spec.rb/event_processor_spec.rb stub the client and will need the new method added to doubles.

title: AgentRun started_at is stamped after the agent finishes — every Slack run records ~0 duration
description: record_run! sets `started_at = Time.current` inside the method, which runs only after AskSavant::Agent#respond has returned (potentially minutes of Ollama calls), then sets finished_at: Time.current a few lines later. Every Slack AgentRun therefore shows a duration of milliseconds regardless of actual runtime. record_run_failure (line 433) has the same problem.
failure_or_value: Latency observability for the Slack agents is fiction: the AgentRun audit trail (the thing Don or drift monitoring would inspect to spot slow turns or Ollama degradation) says every run took ~0s. Any future 'Kerri feels slow' investigation has no data.
fix_sketch: Capture `@run_started_at = Time.current` at the top of EventProcessor#call (right after the actionable checks), and use it for started_at in both record_run! and record_run_failure, keeping finished_at: Time.current. One-line spec: run duration equals the stubbed agent latency.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms the exact claim: EventProcessor#call runs AskSavant::Agent#respond at line 63, then record_run! (line 73) stamps started_at = Time.current at line 401 and finished_at: Time.current at line 413 in the same method, so both timestamps are microseconds apart no matter how long the Ollama turn took; record_run_failure (lines 433-434) repeats the pattern. The bogus value is genuinely surfaced: AgentRun#duration_seconds (agent_run.rb:22-24) renders in agents/show.html.erb and agent_runs/_run_row.html.erb, and run.started_at is exposed to agents via tool_executor.rb:4509. No compensating total-duration exists in RunTelemetry (per-tool ms only). The correct pattern already exists in scheduled_agent_run_job.rb:53-81 (stamp started_at before executing, close with finished_at after), making Slack runs the sole outlier and the fix sketch straightforward.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. Pure timestamp-accuracy fix inside record_run!/record_run_failure: no schema change, no API field rename/removal (started_at only becomes accurate, an additive-compatible semantic correction for agents reading runs via tool_executor), no client-email surface touched (touches_client_email=false). Only watchpoints: capture the start time after the actionable/ignored early-returns so ignored events don't allocate state, and keep external_id dedup and agent.last_run_at behavior unchanged; a spec stubbing agent latency proves the duration.

title: A failed enqueue in handle_envelope tears down the whole Socket Mode connection
description: handle_envelope only rescues JSON::ParserError. AsyncEventDispatch#call runs SlackEventJob.perform_later before the ack; if the Solid Queue insert raises (DB connection blip, pool exhaustion), the exception propagates out of the websocket driver's :message callback, through driver.parse, out of #run — killing the connection for ALL in-flight traffic on that workspace and forcing a full reconnect cycle (2-30s backoff) for one bad event. The envelope also goes un-acked (correct — Slack will redeliver), but every other buffered frame on that connection is lost with it and must wait for redelivery too.
failure_or_value: A 2-second Postgres hiccup while Brian is actively chatting: instead of one message being retried by Slack, the socket drops, the workspace reconnects, and several seconds of messages stall — visible as the bot 'freezing' mid-conversation.
fix_sketch: In handle_envelope, wrap `dispatch.call` in `begin ... rescue => e` for the events_api branch: log the failure and return :dispatch_failed WITHOUT acking (so Slack redelivers just that envelope) and without letting the exception reach driver.parse. Keep the connection alive. Spec: a processor factory whose call raises leaves the connection loop running and does not send an ack frame.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every link in the chain. handle_envelope (app/services/slack/socket_mode_connection.rb:57-77) rescues only JSON::ParserError; AsyncEventDispatch#call (line 28) does SlackEventJob.perform_later, a Solid Queue Postgres INSERT that raises ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError/ConnectionNotEstablished on a DB blip or pool exhaustion. websocket-driver 0.8.2's EventEmitter#emit (event_emitter.rb:37-41) has no rescue around listeners and hybi.rb#emit_message rescues only ExtensionError, so the exception escapes driver.parse. SocketModeConnection#run's rescue (line 51) covers only IO/SSL errors, so the AR error escapes run raw; the ensure closes the socket. SocketModeRunner#run_workspace_forever (socket_mode_runner.rb:55-59) catches it and reconnects after 2-30s backoff. Concrete input: any events_api envelope arriving while the queue-DB insert fails tears down the whole workspace socket instead of failing just that envelope; un-acked envelopes are redelivered but everything in flight stalls through the reconnect. Bonus: the backoff reset at runner line 54 is unreachable (run only exits by raising), so repeated dispatch failures climb straight to the 30s max, amplifying a short DB hiccup. Severity stays low: no data loss (Slack redelivers un-acked envelopes), process survives, and the trigger (DB unavailable in the same process that runs Solid Queue) is uncommon and would degrade job processing anyway.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is a targeted rescue inside handle_envelope's events_api branch in one internal service; no API fields, DB schema, mailers, or client email are touched (touches_client_email=false). Main risk is over-broad swallowing: a bare rescue around dispatch.call could mask a persistently broken enqueue path, leaving the bot connected but silently processing nothing, whereas today's crash-and-reconnect at least logs loudly. Mitigate with error-level logging plus a consecutive-failure counter that falls back to raising (restoring current teardown behavior) after N failures. Also keep the no-ack-on-failure semantics so Slack redelivers; accidentally acking before a failed dispatch would drop the event permanently. Existing spec suite covers handle_envelope's ack ordering, so add the raising-processor-factory spec from the sketch and rerun the full suite.

title: Pull-back ignores the in-flight send claim, so an email can go out after a 'successful' pull-back (double-send risk)
description: SendApprovedDraftsJob durably claims a card by stamping resolution_payload.send_started_at under a row lock (send_approved_drafts_job.rb:157-159), then does slow Drive attachment downloads and the actual Graph/Gmail send OUTSIDE the lock (lines 45-72). TasksController#pull_back (lines 226-239) locks the row but only checks applied_at, not send_started_at, and then resets resolution_payload to {} — wiping the claim and the edited_body. The show page renders the PULL BACK button whenever approved_pending_send? is true, which includes the whole in-flight window.
failure_or_value: Brian approves a card; within the ~2-minute window the job claims it and starts a slow send (Drive fetch + network). Brian taps 'PULL BACK TO EDIT' on his phone: the guard passes (applied_at is nil), the card returns to needs_approval and he's told 'It won't send until you approve it again.' Seconds later send_message completes and stamp_sent! (on the stale in-memory record) forces status done + applied_at — the email already went to the real recipient. If Brian edits and re-approves before noticing, the recipient gets the email twice. The controller comment at line 219-221 says this window 'can't be closed from Rails', but that predates the send_started_at claim, which makes it closable now.
fix_sketch: In pull_back's with_lock block, before the applied_at check, add: if payload["send_started_at"].present? && fresh (< SendApprovedDraftsJob::UNCONFIRMED_SEND_GRACE old) -> set a third flag (e.g. sending_now = true) and redirect with alert 'Kerri is sending this right now; it can't be pulled back.' Stale claims (past the grace window) fall through to the existing hold flow. Also change the reset at line 230 to preserve non-decision payload keys (merge-except resolution keys) instead of wiping to {}, so audit keys like send_unconfirmed_started_at survive. Add a request spec: claim stamped -> pull_back refuses.

verdict.reason: Re-read all cited code. SendApprovedDraftsJob#claim_for_send (job:91-171) commits send_started_at under with_lock then sends OUTSIDE the lock (job:55-72); TasksController#pull_back (controller:226-239) guards only on applied_at (line 227) and wipes resolution_payload to {} (line 230), destroying the claim; the PULL BACK button renders for the entire in-flight window (show.html.erb:191) promising 'It won't send until you approve it again.' Concrete interleaving with no crash: claim commits → Brian pulls back (guard passes, claim wiped) → send completes and stamp_sent! forces done+applied_at → Brian re-approves from his stale page; approve (controller:153-186) has NO status guard and overwrites the payload wholesale (line 174), erasing applied_at → next sweep re-sends. Recipient gets the email twice. Even the milder ordering deterministically sends the OLD draft after a 'successful' pull-back and silently discards Brian's edits. Specs cover only the applied_at guard, no send_started_at case. The controller comment claiming the window 'can't be closed from Rails' predates the claim mechanism and is now wrong.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix makes sending STRICTER (pull_back refuses during a fresh in-flight claim; no new sends, no client-email enablement despite touches_client_email flag — it hardens the existing internal-approved send path). No /api/v1 field renames/removals and no schema change; only controller logic plus payload-key preservation. One edge to handle: if the job dies after claiming but before sending, pull-back is blocked for up to UNCONFIRMED_SEND_GRACE (10 min) until the existing hold_for_unconfirmed_send escalation clears it — acceptable since pulling back during an unconfirmed send is exactly the unsafe case, but the refusal alert should say to wait. Recommend also adding a status guard to approve (reject done cards) to close the second half of the double-send; that guard must not block the legitimate re-approve-after-hold flows (holds reset status to needs_approval, so a simple 'not done' check is safe). Add request specs: fresh claim → pull_back refuses; stale claim → falls through.

title: API create's idempotent-replay path bypasses the completion-proof gate (and can regress live cards)
description: The proof gate from PR #115 (completion_write_allowed?, lines 181-190: moving a task to done via the agent API requires completion_proof or applied_at) is only enforced in #update. #create's idempotent-replay branch (lines 39-53) does existing.update!(refresh_attrs) with the full permitted params — including status — with no gate. The same replay can also overwrite the status of a card that already carries a resolution (e.g. yank an approved-pending-send card in agent_working back to needs_approval by re-filing it), corrupting the send pipeline state.
failure_or_value: An agent with only tasks:write POSTs /api/v1/tasks with an existing external_ref and task[status]=done and no proof: the card silently archives as done with zero completion proof — exactly the done-without-proof failure mode the gate and the QUEUE badge were built to prevent — and Task#run_on_complete_action fires (resolution is not 'skipped'), so an on_complete like create_deal executes even though nothing was actually done. Agents retry create calls constantly (that's what external_ref idempotency is for), so this path is hit in normal operation, not just adversarially.
fix_sketch: In the replay branch: (1) run the same completion_write_allowed?(existing.status) check before existing.update! when refresh_attrs['status'] == 'done' and the card isn't already done; (2) drop 'status' from refresh_attrs when existing.resolution.present? (a resolved/parked card's state machine belongs to the decision pipeline, not re-filing); (3) keep everything else additive so agent callers see no field changes. Add specs for both cases.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms both failure modes on the real code. (1) completion_write_allowed? (tasks_controller.rb:181) is invoked only from #update (line 74); the #create idempotent-replay branch (lines 39-53) calls existing.update!(task_params.except(:external_ref)) with :status permitted (line 155) and no gate. Concrete input: POST /api/v1/tasks with an existing external_ref and task[status]=done, key with only tasks:write — no resolution keys so resolution_write_requested? is false and tasks:resolve isn't required. The card archives done with zero proof, and Task's after_commit run_on_complete_action (task.rb:82,159-164) fires because done? and saved_change_to_status? are true and resolution is nil (TaskCompletionAction only skips on resolution=="skipped", task_completion_action.rb:86), so a create_deal on_complete executes on unproven work. The identical PATCH body is rejected 422 by an existing spec (tasks_spec.rb:188), proving the asymmetry is unintended. (2) The regression scenario is confirmed and worse than claimed: replaying a create (normal agent retry, original status needs_approval) against a card Brian approved (agent_working + resolution approved, no applied_at) sets status back to needs_approval while resolution stays approved — a state matching neither open_board (task.rb:50-56 requires agent_working for the approved branch) nor approved_pending_send (task.rb:63-66), so the card vanishes from the board AND drops out of SendApprovedDraftsJob's queue; the approved draft silently never sends. No model validation, state-machine guard, or spec covers the replay-with-status path. Severity high: defeats the PR #115 proof regime (creates the exact done-without-proof state the QUEUE badge polices), triggers side effects like create_deal without proof, and can silently strand approved sends via the retry path agents use constantly.
verdict.ship_risk: Low, if implemented as sketched. The fix is server-side gating only: (a) run completion_write_allowed?(existing.status) in the replay branch before update!, (b) drop 'status' from refresh_attrs when existing.resolution.present?. No API fields are renamed or removed and the response shape (data + meta.idempotent_replay) is unchanged, so agent pollers are unaffected. Behavioral compat risks to watch: an agent that replays create with status=done AND valid proof still passes the gate (proof check reads the same params), so legitimate closers are fine; an agent that relied on re-filing to flip a resolved card's column would now be no-op'd, which is the intended correction — worth one release-note line and specs for both cases. The sync glue that stamps applied_at uses PATCH (#update), not create-replay, so it is untouched. touches_client_email=false: no mailer or sponsor-facing send is anywhere near this path (tasks controller + TaskCompletionAction create_deal only), and the fix adds no email behavior.

title: Held cards (numeric mismatch, sign-off mismatch, unconfirmed send, missing attachments) look identical to fresh cards on the board and review page
description: SendApprovedDraftsJob bounces unsendable approved cards back to needs_approval with resolution_payload.held_reason / held_detail (numeric_ground_truth, signoff_mismatch, send_unconfirmed, attachments_unresolved). No view renders these keys anywhere (rg confirms only the job writes them). The only trace is a 'held' TaskEvent buried at the bottom of the proof trail, below the draft. The kanban card shows a plain REVIEW chip like any new card.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: Brian on his phone sees a card back in Needs approval, assumes Kerri filed a fresh draft, and taps APPROVE & SEND without reading the proof trail. For held_reason=send_unconfirmed that is exactly the dangerous move — the hold text says 'check the Sent folder before re-approving' because the email may already have gone out; blind re-approval risks a double send to a sponsor. For numeric_ground_truth he re-sends a dollar figure that contradicts the CRM. A visible banner turns a silent trap into a one-glance decision.
fix_sketch: In show.html.erb, right above the resolution panel (line 44), render a warn-styled panel when @task.resolution_payload.to_h['held_reason'].present?: headline per reason ('Held before send — do not re-approve until you check the Sent folder' for send_unconfirmed) + held_detail text; clear styling reuses the existing panel !border-warn classes. In _kanban_card.html.erb add a small 'HELD: <reason>' chip (same spot as the approved_pending_send? note, line 51). Display-only; no schema or API change. Clear the banner naturally: approve/skip already overwrite resolution_payload.

verdict.reason: Verified against the real code. All four hold paths in /Users/brianderario/Projects/kerrihq-rails/app/jobs/send_approved_drafts_job.rb (hold_for_numeric_mismatch! L194-205, hold_for_signoff_mismatch! L211-223, hold_for_unconfirmed_send! L262-278, hold_for_missing_attachments! L319+) set status back to needs_approval with resolution: nil and write held_reason/held_detail into resolution_payload. rg across app/ confirms NO view, helper, serializer, or API endpoint reads held_reason/held_detail — only the job writes them and specs assert them. On tasks/show.html.erb the resolution banner at L44 requires @task.resolution.present?, which the hold explicitly nils, so a held card renders the exact same "What approving does" accent panel (L50-55) and the same sticky APPROVE & SEND bar (L142-148, always on screen on a phone) as a brand-new card; the turbo_confirm text carries no held warning. _kanban_card.html.erb shows a plain REVIEW link (L27) with no held indicator. The only trace is the "held" TaskEvent — one nuance vs. the finding: TaskEvent.recent orders occurred_at desc, so the held note is at the TOP of the proof trail, not the bottom; but the trail panel itself sits below the draft and thread frame, well below the fold, so the substance stands. Concrete dangerous path confirmed: hold_for_unconfirmed_send! clears send_started_at (keeping only send_unconfirmed_started_at), so a blind re-approve sends immediately with no further guard — the double-send risk to a sponsor is real, and the "check the Sent folder" instruction lives only in the buried event note. The fix sketch is sound: approve (tasks_controller.rb L160-174), skip (L190-191), redo (L205), and pull_back (L230) all REPLACE resolution_payload wholesale, so a display-only banner keyed on resolution_payload['held_reason'] clears naturally on any action with zero extra state.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Display-only change to two ERB views; no migration, no controller/job logic change, no new state. API backward-compat: untouched (held_reason already lives inside resolution_payload; rendering it adds no API field, and if later exposed it would be additive). Client-email: does not touch any send path — if anything it reduces the chance of an accidental duplicate sponsor send; touches_client_email=false is correct. Residual risks: (1) keep the banner condition scoped to resolution.blank? so a stale key can never show on a resolved card (all resolution paths already replace the payload, so this is belt-and-braces); (2) reuse existing warn panel classes (!border-warn, bg-warn/5 pattern already used at show.html.erb L96) so no Tailwind purge surprises; (3) the kanban HELD chip must not break the shared kanban_controller.js dataset contract (data-deal-id etc.) — it's additive markup, so it won't. Test-suite impact: none of the existing specs assert the absence of this markup; add a view/request spec for the banner.

title: TaskQueueHealth runs an unbounded N+1 over every done agent task on every page render (topbar badge)
