In Ruby the env hash is MERGED into, not substituted for, the parent process environment (verified: a child spawned with `{"HOME"=>"/tmp"}` still saw a probe var set in the parent). So every workspace command inherits the Render container's real secrets — GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN, RENDER_API_KEY, DATABASE_URL, SENDGRID_*, master key material, etc. Combined with the CommandPolicy denylist gap above, any command can read them; even without that gap, a compromised or buggy toolchain command has ambient access to production credentials it should never see.
failure_or_value: A workspace command such as `sh -c 'set'` or a Ruby-based tool step prints/uses the inherited RENDER_API_KEY or GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN; the value lands in event stdout/stderr and the DB, and is returned to the agent — a credential that grants deploy/rollback and code-write on the repo.
fix_sketch: Pass `unsetenv_others: true` to Open3.popen3 so only safe_env is present, and explicitly whitelist just the vars the toolchain needs (PATH, HOME, CI, RAILS_ENV, NODE_ENV, BUNDLE_*). Ensure GITHUB_*, RENDER_*, DATABASE_URL, SENDGRID_*, and master key are never in safe_env.

verdict.reason: Re-reading runner.rb:192, Open3.popen3(safe_env, *argv, ...) is called with no unsetenv_others:true, which is standard Ruby merge-not-replace behavior: the child inherits the parent Render container's full ENV (GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN, RENDER_API_KEY, DATABASE_URL, SENDGRID_*, RAILS_MASTER_KEY) plus the safe_env overrides. safe_env (259-271) only ADDS 7 keys and never scrubs the rest. CommandPolicy narrows read vectors but does not close them: it blocks bare env/printenv (\b(printenv|env)\b), shell meta [|;&`$<>], and curl/wget/nc, but NOT sh/bash/awk. Concrete confirmed inputs: `sh -c set` (argv ["sh","-c","set"], no meta, no secret-word match) prints all imported env vars including secrets to stdout, which is captured into the command event at runner.rb:113 and returned to the agent; `awk 'BEGIN{for(k in ENVIRON) print k, ENVIRON[k]}'` also passes (\benv\b doesn't match ENVIRON, braces/parens aren't in the meta class) and dumps the whole environment. So production deploy/code-write credentials are exfiltrable by an agent- or injection-authored command. Both the ambient-authority design flaw and a concrete leak path are real.
verdict.ship_risk: No client-email exposure. The main risk is breaking the self-upgrade eval itself: per the runner.rb:248-256 comment and safe_env, the sandbox runs the eval suite in production RAILS_ENV, which requires DATABASE_URL to connect and RAILS_MASTER_KEY/SECRET_KEY_BASE to boot Rails. A naive `unsetenv_others: true` with only the current 7-key safe_env would strand every bundler/rails command and fail DB connection, defeating the runner's purpose (this is exactly the failure mode the comment says stranded the first live sandbox run). The correct fix must explicitly whitelist toolchain/eval necessities (DATABASE_URL, RAILS_MASTER_KEY or SECRET_KEY_BASE, GEM_HOME/GEM_PATH, LANG/LC_*, SSL_CERT_FILE, TMPDIR) while excluding the true deploy/API/code-write tokens (GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN, RENDER_API_KEY, SENDGRID_*). No API/schema backward-compat concerns. Requires a live production self-upgrade dry-run to confirm the eval suite still boots and connects after scrubbing.

title: Sandbox edit engine uses 2-arg String#sub/gsub, so it tests different bytes than CodeShippingClient ships
description: WorkspaceRunner#apply_edit! applies edits with `content.gsub(old_string, new_string)` / `content.sub(old_string, new_string)` — the two-argument form, which interprets backreference sequences (`\0`, `\1`, `\&`, `\k<name>`, `\\`) inside new_string. CodeShippingClient#apply_string_edit deliberately uses the block form `content.sub(old_string) { new_string }` (see its comment) precisely to treat those sequences literally. The sandbox is described as having 'one irreplaceable job' — running the behavioral eval against THE EDITED CODE — but when new_string contains a backslash sequence (common in real code: regex replacements, Windows paths, escaped `\n`, sprintf specs), the sandbox writes corrupted text while the PR step ships the correct text. Verified: `"abc OLD def".sub("OLD","X\\0Y")` => `"abc XOLDY def"` vs block form `"abc X\\0Y def"`.
failure_or_value: An autonomous self-upgrade edits system_prompt.rb with a new_string containing `\1`; the sandbox eval runs against text where `\1` was replaced by the empty capture group (silently deleting it) and passes, but CodeShippingClient ships the literal `\1`. The 'verified in sandbox' guarantee is voided — sandbox-green code is not the code that deploys.
fix_sketch: Change line 94 to the block form matching CodeShippingClient: `updated = replace_all ? content.gsub(old_string) { new_string } : content.sub(old_string) { new_string }`.

verdict.reason: Re-read both files: workspace_runner/runner.rb:94 uses 2-arg sub/gsub while code_shipping_client.rb:543 deliberately uses the block form (its comment at 541-542 explains why). self_upgrades/runner.rb passes the identical upgrade.edits to both the sandbox WorkspaceRun (line 79) and CodeShippingClient#start_task (line 141), so the sandbox gate can evaluate different bytes than the PR ships. Reproduced concretely with Ruby: new_string "\1\1" applied over a line containing gsub(/(a)/, "\1") yields "" in the sandbox (backrefs resolve to nil) but the correct "\1\1" via the block form. Triggers include \0, \1-\9, \&, \\, \k<name> in new_string, all realistic in code edits. Downgraded from high to medium: most divergences either fail rubocop/eval in the sandbox (false red, a reliability annoyance) or need the corrupted variant to still pass the full gate for a silent green-then-divergent ship, which narrows the truly dangerous window. Still real because it voids the sandbox's single invariant (eval ran against the exact shipped edits) and also affects agent-driven workspace runs via the Ask Savant tool executor and /api/v1/workspace_runs.
verdict.ship_risk: Very low. One-line change in an internal sandbox service to match CodeShippingClient's existing literal-replacement semantics; no API field renames, no schema change, no client-email surface (touches_client_email=false). Only behavior change: an edit that (implausibly) relied on backref expansion in the sandbox would now be applied literally, which is exactly what ships anyway, so consistency improves. Add a regression test with a backslash-sequence new_string to lock the parity in.

title: Failed `git clone` stderr is stored and returned unsanitized, leaking the tokenized clone URL
description: RepositorySource.clone_url embeds `x-access-token:<GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN>@github.com` in the clone URL passed as argv. On clone failure, git often echoes the full remote URL (including the token) in its fatal/unable-to-access error text. prepare_workspace! stores raw result[:stderr] on the event (line 61) and interpolates it into the raised Error (line 62). sanitize_source is applied only to the metadata `source` field, NOT to stdout/stderr. That stderr is persisted to the DB and surfaced to the agent via read_workspace_run, so an auth/network failure during clone can leak the code-write token.
failure_or_value: A transient 403 or DNS failure on clone produces `fatal: unable to access 'https://x-access-token:ghs_xxx@github.com/kerrihq/kerrihq-rails.git/'` in stderr; that token string is written to workspace_run_events.stderr and returned to the agent/logs.
fix_sketch: Run result[:stdout]/result[:stderr] through sanitize_source (or a shared redactor covering x-access-token:...@ and any Bearer tokens) before storing on the event and before interpolating into the raised Error. Consider using a git credential helper / GIT_ASKPASS instead of an inline-URL token.

verdict.reason: The core defect is real, but the finding's named trigger is partly wrong, so I verified empirically. Code structure matches the claim exactly: WorkspaceRunner::RepositorySource.clone_url (repository_source.rb:25) embeds GITHUB_CODE_WRITE_TOKEN as `https://x-access-token:<token>@github.com/...`; Runner#prepare_workspace! (runner.rb:61) persists raw result[:stderr]/[:stdout] to workspace_run_events and interpolates stderr into the raised Error (runner.rb:62), which fail_run! stores in run.error; sanitize_source is applied ONLY to metadata.source (runner.rb:280-282). All of that flows back to agents verbatim: AskSavant::ToolExecutor#serialize_workspace_run returns event.stdout/event.stderr and run.error unredacted (tool_executor.rb:4508, 4522-4523) via read_workspace_run. HOWEVER, the claimed leak vector is refuted: I ran the exact argv shape against git 2.39 and modern git anonymizes the URL userinfo in every clone-failure stderr path tested (auth failure prints `fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://github.com/...'` with credentials stripped; DNS failure prints `fatal: unable to access 'https://host/...'` stripped; missing-branch failure prints no URL at all). So a 403/DNS clone failure does NOT leak the token on any remotely modern git. The leak is nonetheless concretely reproducible on the real code path via a different door in the same subsystem: `git clone` persists the tokenized URL into the checkout's `.git/config` (empirically verified), and CommandPolicy (command_policy.rb:13-15) does not block the `remote` or `config` git subcommands and its SECRET_PATTERNS don't match them — so an agent-submitted run with commands: ["git remote -v"] (or `git config --get remote.origin.url`) writes the raw token into event stdout (verified locally: `origin https://fakeuser:ghs_FAKETOKEN123@github.com/... (fetch)`), which is persisted and returned to the agent. The finding's fix sketch (shared redactor over stdout/stderr covering `x-access-token:...@` and gh*_ token shapes before event.finish! and before raising) is the right fix and closes the confirmed vector too; additionally scrub the credential from the remote after clone (`git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<repo>.git` — safe since the runner never fetches again) and add `remote`/`config` to the git-subcommand blocklist. Severity stays medium: exposure requires an org agent workspace run (human-confirmed via the start_workspace_run gate), but the leaked credential is a GitHub code-write token landing in DB rows and agent/LLM context.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is purely defensive and additive: redacting token patterns inside existing stdout/stderr/error string values changes no API field names or shapes, so agent pollers of /api/v1 and read_workspace_run are unaffected (they just see `[redacted]` where a secret would have been). No client email surface anywhere near this path (touches_client_email=false). No schema change needed. Two watch-items: (1) keep the redaction regex targeted (x-access-token:[^@\s]+@, ghs_/ghp_/github_pat_ token shapes) so legitimate output mentioning github.com isn't mangled and diffs/test output pass through intact; (2) if also scrubbing the remote URL post-clone, do it only after a successful clone and don't switch to a credential-helper rewrite in the same change — the inline-URL clone is what currently works on Render, and swapping auth mechanisms carries real breakage risk for the live self-upgrade sandbox, so ship redaction first and treat GIT_ASKPASS/credential-helper as a separate follow-up.

title: Tier classifier and edit path handling can be fooled by `..` traversal, mislabeling a protected file as autonomous
description: SelfUpgrade.classify_tier does prefix matching on raw, unnormalized edit paths. A path like `docs/../app/services/ask_savant/access_policy.rb` starts_with the ALLOWED prefix `docs/` and does NOT start_with any PROTECTED prefix (which begin `app/...`), so it classifies as `autonomous` and skips the harness_change human approval. CodeEditPreflight (which uses File.expand_path, collapsing `..`) still finds the real protected file and passes if old_string matches, and WorkspaceRunner#safe_workspace_file uses cleanpath so the sandbox actually applies the edit to the protected file. The end-to-end merge is currently backstopped because CodeShippingClient#validate_edit! rejects paths containing `..`, so the PR step fails — but the safety-rail CLASSIFIER itself is bypassed: an agent can drive the sandbox to run against a modified copy of access_policy.rb / self_upgrades pipeline code with no human approval, and the defense rests entirely on one downstream string check.
failure_or_value: self_upgrade with edit path `docs/../app/services/ask_savant/access_policy.rb` is classified `autonomous`, no approval is filed, the sandbox checks out and applies the edit to the real access_policy.rb and runs the eval; only the later `..` rejection in CodeShippingClient stops the merge.
fix_sketch: Normalize each edit path (reject any containing `..` or leading `/`, then Pathname#cleanpath) in SelfUpgrade#touched_paths / classify_tier before prefix matching, and add the same `..` rejection to WorkspaceRunner (UNSAFE_PATH_PATTERN) and self_upgrade tool input so the classifier sees the same canonical path the sandbox writes.

verdict.reason: Every step reproduces on the real code path with the concrete input `docs/../app/services/ask_savant/access_policy.rb`. (1) Classifier: `SelfUpgrade.classify_tier` (app/models/self_upgrade.rb:85-90) does raw `start_with?` on unnormalized paths; I executed the exact logic and the traversal path classifies `autonomous` (matches ALLOWED `docs/`, matches no PROTECTED prefix since those all begin `app/`, `.github/`, `config/`, `db/`, `Gemfile`). (2) Gate skip: `SelfUpgrades::Runner.propose!` (app/services/self_upgrades/runner.rb:38,54-59) files NO harness_change ApprovalRequest for autonomous — it goes straight to `start_sandbox!`. (3) Preflight passes: `CodeEditPreflight#resolve` (app/services/code_edit_preflight.rb:72-75) uses `File.expand_path`, which collapses `..` and stays inside Rails.root; `CodeContext::DENY_PATH_PATTERNS` (app/services/code_context.rb:12-25) has no `..` rule; old_string is checked against the REAL protected file so a verbatim copy passes. (4) Sandbox applies it: `WorkspaceRunner::Runner#safe_workspace_file` (runner.rb:163-173) — `UNSAFE_PATH_PATTERN` (line 17) doesn't match `..` (verified), and `root.join(path).cleanpath` resolves to the real `app/services/ask_savant/access_policy.rb` inside the checkout, so the edit lands on the protected file and `bin/rails eval:agent` runs in RAILS_ENV=production against attacker-chosen modifications to a protected file — and Open3.popen3's env-hash MERGES with the parent process env, so production secrets are inherited by that run. The ledger and audit records mislabel the whole thing `autonomous`. (5) Backstop confirmed as claimed: `CodeShippingClient#validate_edit!` (code_shipping_client.rb:481, ConfigurationError < Error at lines 10-11) rejects `..`, so `ship!` fails and no unapproved merge occurs. Net: the finding is accurate including its own caveat — the safety-rail classifier and approval gate are bypassed, unapproved execution against modified protected code happens in the sandbox, and the merge defense rests on a single downstream string check. Kept at medium rather than high because (a) the end-to-end merge IS blocked, (b) exploitation requires code_shipping_role (Brian-direct or teammate + confirm, and the confirm payload displays the raw `docs/../...` path), and (c) the autonomous tier already permits arbitrary new_string Ruby to run in the sandbox for genuinely allowed files by design — the marginal escalation is the tier mislabel, skipped approval, and single-point-of-failure defense, which is exactly a defense-in-depth hole in the system's own 'never her cage' invariant (self_upgrade.rb:28,37-39).
verdict.ship_risk: Low. The fix is pure input hardening: reject paths containing `..` or leading `/` and cleanpath-normalize before prefix matching in SelfUpgrade.classify_tier/touched_paths, plus add `..` to WorkspaceRunner's UNSAFE_PATH_PATTERN. No legitimate caller uses traversal paths (CodeShippingClient already rejects them at ship time, so any such upgrade was doomed anyway), so nothing working today breaks. Zero client-email surface (touches_client_email=false — this is the self-upgrade pipeline, nowhere near sponsor mail). Zero /api/v1 field or DB schema changes — validation-only, additive. Main care points: (1) normalize consistently in BOTH touched_paths and classify_tier so the ledger, approval payload, and sandbox all see the same canonical path; (2) reject rather than silently normalize in the self_upgrade tool input so the agent gets a clear error instead of a surprise tier; (3) add regression specs for classify_tier with `docs/../...`, absolute paths, and `./`-prefixed paths, and confirm the existing green suite still passes (existing specs presumably only cover clean paths, so no expected breakage).

title: Successful autonomous self-upgrades deploy to production with no owner notification
description: The self-upgrade pipeline notifies the owner (via tasks.create!) on every FAILURE path (sandbox fail, PR fail, CI timeout/fail, deploy fail, canary rollback), but there is no notification on the SUCCESS path. When an autonomous-tier upgrade (Kerri editing her own prompt/tools/docs) passes sandbox + CI, auto-merges to main, deploys via Render, and verifies through canary, status is set to :verified silently with zero signal to Brian. For a non-technical CEO who governs by 'my account of it,' Kerri shipping and deploying code to production unattended with no record surfaced to him is a governance/observability gap, not just a missing nicety.
failure_or_value: Every green autonomous self-upgrade changes live agent behavior with no task, Slack, or email to the owner — Brian has no timeline of what Kerri changed about herself unless he polls self_upgrade_status. Adding a success notification gives him an auditable, phone-visible record of each autonomous prod deploy.
fix_sketch: In SelfUpgradeCanaryJob when transitioning to :verified (line 48), call a notify! with a non-urgent status (e.g. informational task and/or Slack DM) summarizing reason, paths, PR number, and merge sha. Optionally gate autonomous-tier merges behind a lightweight after-the-fact digest so Brian always sees a one-line 'Kerri self-upgraded: <reason>' entry.

verdict.reason: Re-read confirms the asymmetry: every failure path creates an owner task (canary_job.rb:35/66/119 via notify!, runner.rb:129/150/156/172/178 via notify_failure!) but the success transition at self_upgrade_canary_job.rb:46-48 just sets status :verified silently. No compensating surface exists: no self_upgrade views/controllers/routes, the audit! row is written at proposal time only, and self_upgrade_status is a pull-only agent tool. The confirm gate in tool_executor.rb:1360 is prompt-level (agent can pass confirm:true itself), so an autonomous-tier upgrade to Kerri's own prompt/tools can merge and deploy to production with zero push signal to Brian. The notify! helper already exists in the same job, so the upgrade is real, high-value for a governance-by-account owner, and trivially feasible. Kept at medium (not high) because the safety story (canary rollback, watchdog, kill switch) is intact — this is observability, not a safety hole.
verdict.ship_risk: Low. Purely additive internal notification: reuses the existing notify!/tasks.create! path in the same job, touches no client email (touches_client_email=false), no /api/v1 field changes, no schema changes. Two small cautions: (1) reusing notify! as-is would file the success with status :action_needed, cluttering Brian's approval queue — use an informational/done status or a distinct title so successes don't demand action; (2) minor duplicate-task risk if the job retries between update!(status: :verified) and the task create, same exposure the existing failure paths already accept. Note the file lives under PROTECTED_PATHS (app/jobs/self_upgrade), so if Kerri ships this herself it correctly requires Brian's approval.
